questions.stem: A 65-year-old woman comes to the clinic complaining of new-onset muscle aches. She was recently started on an antihyperlipidemic agent. Which of the following best describes the lipid-lowering mechanism of her prescribed medication?

choices.label: C
choices.text: Preventing intestinal absorption of bile acids

explanation.summary: Statins lower LDL primarily by increasing hepatic LDL-receptor expression.
explanation.whyCorrect: By inhibiting HMG-CoA reductase, statins reduce intracellular cholesterol synthesis. The resulting fall in hepatic cholesterol upregulates plasma-membrane LDL receptors, which pull LDL out of the blood and lower circulating LDL-C. Myalgia (statin-associated muscle symptoms) is a common adverse effect and fits this class.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Inhibiting hormone-sensitive lipase is not the mechanism of statins.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Blocking bile-acid absorption describes bile-acid sequestrants.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Preventing intestinal cholesterol absorption is the mechanism of ezetimibe, not statins.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Upregulating lipoprotein lipase describes fibrates, not statins.

questions.stem: What is the primary molecular mechanism by which statins reduce LDL levels?

explanation.summary: Statins inhibit HMG-CoA reductase, the rate-limiting enzyme of cholesterol synthesis.
explanation.whyCorrect: HMG-CoA reductase catalyzes the rate-limiting step in the pathway that ultimately forms cholesterol. Statins occupy the substrate-binding site of the enzyme; the resulting drop in cholesterol synthesis upregulates hepatic LDL receptors and lowers circulating LDL-C.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Activating lipoprotein lipase is not the statin mechanism.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Statins modestly increase (not decrease) HDL, and this is not how they lower LDL.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Statins decrease circulating VLDL rather than increase it.
whyWrongByChoice.D: There is no 'acetyl-CoA reductase' step blocked by statins; the target is HMG-CoA reductase.

questions.stem: A patient is being counseled about potential drug interactions with a statin that is extensively metabolized by CYP3A4. Which of the following statins is metabolized by CYP3A4?

explanation.summary: Simvastatin is metabolized by CYP3A4.
explanation.whyCorrect: Simvastatin (like lovastatin and atorvastatin) is extensively metabolized by CYP3A4, so CYP3A4 inhibitors raise its levels and increase myopathy risk.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Fluvastatin clearance is partly dependent on CYP2C9, not CYP3A4.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Pitavastatin undergoes minimal hepatic metabolism.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Pravastatin is cleared primarily by non-CYP450 transformations.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Rosuvastatin is cleared primarily by non-CYP450 (OATP transporter) pathways.

questions.stem: A patient with a history of statin-associated muscle symptoms needs a statin whose hydrophilic nature lowers the risk of muscle toxicity. Which of the following statins is hydrophilic?

explanation.summary: Pravastatin is hydrophilic, which is associated with a lower risk of statin-associated muscle symptoms (SAMS).
explanation.whyCorrect: Pravastatin and rosuvastatin are hydrophilic statins and therefore carry a lower risk of SAMS. Because pravastatin is the only hydrophilic option listed, it is the best answer.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Atorvastatin is lipophilic and carries a higher SAMS risk.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Lovastatin is lipophilic and carries a higher SAMS risk.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Pitavastatin is lipophilic, so it does not fit the hydrophilic criterion asked about here.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Simvastatin is lipophilic and carries a higher SAMS risk.

questions.stem: A patient taking simvastatin to lower cholesterol asks about dietary precautions. It is best to advise the patient not to consume large amounts of which of the following?

explanation.summary: Grapefruit juice inhibits intestinal CYP3A4 and raises simvastatin levels.
explanation.whyCorrect: Because simvastatin is metabolized by CYP3A4, large amounts of grapefruit juice inhibit intestinal CYP3A4 and increase simvastatin concentrations, raising the risk of adverse effects such as myopathy. Rosuvastatin, pravastatin, or pitavastatin are recommended for patients who consume large amounts of grapefruit.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Apple juice does not meaningfully inhibit CYP3A4 or interact with simvastatin metabolism.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Orange juice (unlike grapefruit) does not significantly inhibit intestinal CYP3A4.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Spinach does not inhibit CYP3A4-mediated simvastatin metabolism.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Watermelon juice does not interfere with simvastatin metabolism.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man on a high-dose statin presents with severe muscle pain and weakness. Laboratory studies show a markedly elevated creatine phosphokinase (CPK), dark urine positive for myoglobin, and a rising serum creatinine. Which of the following statin-associated muscle findings best describes his presentation?

explanation.summary: Markedly elevated CPK with myoglobinuria and acute kidney injury indicates rhabdomyolysis, the most severe form of SAMS.
explanation.whyCorrect: Clinical rhabdomyolysis is defined by significantly elevated CPK with myoglobinuria and acute kidney injury, exactly as seen here. It is the most severe end of the statin-associated muscle symptom (SAMS) spectrum.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Diarrhea is a common gastrointestinal adverse effect, unrelated to this muscle presentation.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Hepatic dysfunction presents with elevated liver aminotransferases, not muscle breakdown and myoglobinuria.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Myalgia is muscle aches, soreness, tenderness, or cramps without the markedly elevated CPK, myoglobinuria, or kidney injury described.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Myositis refers to muscle inflammation and does not by itself produce myoglobinuria with acute kidney injury.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man taking simvastatin 40 mg daily is started on amiodarone for atrial fibrillation. Two weeks later he develops diffuse muscle pain. Which of the following best explains the increased risk of myopathy in this patient?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Amiodarone displaces simvastatin from plasma albumin

choices.label: B
choices.text: Amiodarone increases renal clearance of simvastatin metabolites

choices.label: C
choices.text: Amiodarone induces CYP3A4, lowering simvastatin levels

choices.label: D
choices.text: Amiodarone inhibits CYP2C9, the main enzyme for simvastatin

choices.label: E
choices.text: Amiodarone inhibits CYP3A4, increasing simvastatin levels

explanation.summary: Amiodarone inhibits CYP3A4, raising simvastatin levels and increasing myopathy risk.
explanation.whyCorrect: Amiodarone is an antiarrhythmic that inhibits CYP3A4 metabolism. Because simvastatin is a CYP3A4 substrate, its levels rise, and the risk of myopathy and rhabdomyolysis increases with simvastatin doses greater than 20 mg/day when combined with amiodarone.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The interaction is metabolic (CYP3A4 inhibition), not protein-binding displacement.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Increased renal clearance would lower levels and reduce toxicity, the opposite of what occurs.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Amiodarone inhibits rather than induces CYP3A4, so simvastatin levels rise, not fall.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Simvastatin is metabolized by CYP3A4, not CYP2C9.

questions.stem: A patient is being counseled that a particular statin has a short half-life and works best when its dose coincides with peak overnight cholesterol synthesis. Which of the following statins is best taken in the evening?

explanation.summary: Simvastatin has a short half-life and is best taken in the evening.
explanation.whyCorrect: Simvastatin has a short elimination half-life (about 2 to 3 hours), so its optimal time of administration is the evening to maximize efficacy. This is an important counseling pearl.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Atorvastatin has a long half-life (about 15 to 30 hours) and can be taken anytime.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Pitavastatin can be administered anytime.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Pravastatin can be administered anytime.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Rosuvastatin has a long half-life (about 19 hours) and can be taken anytime.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old woman with hyperlipidemia and known hepatic dysfunction needs statin therapy. Which of the following statins undergoes minimal hepatic metabolism and can be used in a patient with hepatic insufficiency?

explanation.summary: Pitavastatin has minimal hepatic metabolism, making it useful in hepatic dysfunction.
explanation.whyCorrect: Pitavastatin undergoes minimal hepatic metabolism, so it can be used in patients with hepatic dysfunction where extensively liver-metabolized statins are less desirable.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Atorvastatin is metabolized by hepatic CYP3A4.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Fluvastatin is metabolized by hepatic CYP2C9.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Lovastatin is metabolized by hepatic CYP3A4.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Simvastatin is extensively metabolized by hepatic CYP3A4.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old man started on a statin six months ago is found to have a new rise in fasting blood glucose consistent with new-onset diabetes. Which of the following best explains how statin therapy can contribute to this finding?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Blockade of GLUT4 transporters in skeletal muscle

choices.label: B
choices.text: Destruction of pancreatic beta-cells by an autoimmune mechanism

choices.label: C
choices.text: Increased glucagon release from pancreatic alpha-cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: Increased LDL uptake in pancreatic beta-cells causing lipotoxicity

choices.label: E
choices.text: Stimulation of hepatic gluconeogenesis by inhibiting HMG-CoA reductase

explanation.summary: Statins can impair glycemic control through increased LDL uptake and lipotoxicity in pancreatic beta-cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: Just as statins upregulate LDL receptors in the liver and increase LDL-C uptake, the same occurs in the pancreas. Increased LDL uptake raises the chance of lipotoxicity in the beta-cells, resulting in decreased insulin secretion and loss of glycemic control, which can unmask or worsen diabetes.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Statin-induced hyperglycemia is not due to GLUT4 blockade in muscle.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Statins cause beta-cell lipotoxicity, not autoimmune beta-cell destruction.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Increased alpha-cell glucagon release is not the described mechanism.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Statins do not raise glucose by stimulating hepatic gluconeogenesis through HMG-CoA reductase inhibition.

questions.stem: According to AHA/ACC guidelines, statins are classified by their estimated LDL-C reduction. Which of the following regimens is a high-intensity statin expected to lower LDL-C by more than 50%?

explanation.summary: Rosuvastatin 20 to 40 mg is a high-intensity statin that lowers LDL-C by more than 50%.
explanation.whyCorrect: High-intensity statins lower LDL-C by more than 50% and include rosuvastatin 20 to 40 mg and atorvastatin 40 to 80 mg. Rosuvastatin 20 mg qualifies as high-intensity.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Atorvastatin 10 to 20 mg is moderate-intensity (30% to 49% reduction), not high-intensity.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Fluvastatin 20 to 40 mg is low-intensity (less than 30% reduction).
whyWrongByChoice.C: Pravastatin 40 to 80 mg is moderate-intensity.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Simvastatin 20 to 40 mg is moderate-intensity.

questions.stem: A 31-year-old woman taking atorvastatin for hypercholesterolemia informs her physician that she has just discovered she is pregnant. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in her lipid management?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Continue atorvastatin at the same dose

choices.label: C
choices.text: Increase the atorvastatin dose for tighter control

choices.label: D
choices.text: Reduce the atorvastatin dose by half

explanation.summary: Statins should be discontinued in pregnancy.
explanation.whyCorrect: Statins should be discontinued in pregnant patients, and breastfeeding is not recommended in patients taking a statin. Therefore the statin should be stopped.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Continuing the statin exposes the pregnancy to a contraindicated drug.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Increasing the dose worsens fetal exposure to a contraindicated agent.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Dose reduction does not make statin therapy acceptable in pregnancy; it should be stopped.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Switching to another statin (rosuvastatin) is still contraindicated in pregnancy.

questions.stem: A 44-year-old man with no complaints comes for a health maintenance visit. He has no chest pain, dyspnea, or exercise intolerance. A fasting lipid profile shows an LDL cholesterol of 190 mg/dL. Which of the following best describes the typical clinical presentation of hyperlipidemia?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Asymptomatic and detected on routine screening tests

choices.label: B
choices.text: Exertional chest pain at the time of diagnosis

choices.label: D
choices.text: Proximal muscle weakness with dark urine

choices.label: E
choices.text: Recurrent watery diarrhea after fatty meals

explanation.summary: Hyperlipidemia is usually asymptomatic and is commonly detected by screening tests during a routine checkup.
explanation.whyCorrect: Hyperlipidemia does not produce symptoms on its own; it is typically found on screening during a routine visit. Over time, however, it can lead to atherosclerosis and thereby raise the risk of cardiovascular disease, chest pain, myocardial infarction, and stroke. Hyperlipidemia contributes to roughly one-third of deaths in middle-aged adults.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Chest pain is a late downstream complication of atherosclerosis, not the usual presentation at diagnosis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Aminotransferase elevation is a hepatic adverse effect of statins, not a presenting feature of hyperlipidemia.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Muscle weakness with myoglobinuria describes statin-associated rhabdomyolysis, not the lipid disorder itself.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Diarrhea is a gastrointestinal adverse effect of statin therapy, not a manifestation of hyperlipidemia.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old man with dyslipidemia has an LDL cholesterol of 170 mg/dL and triglycerides of 210 mg/dL. He is started on a statin. Which of the following best explains the expected reduction in his triglyceride level with this drug?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Blockade of chylomicron formation in the enterocyte

choices.label: C
choices.text: Inhibition of hormone-sensitive lipase in adipose tissue

choices.label: E
choices.text: Upregulation of lipoprotein lipase on capillary endothelium

explanation.summary: Statins lower triglycerides by decreasing circulating VLDL, producing roughly a 20-40% reduction in TG.
explanation.whyCorrect: Beyond lowering LDL-C, statins decrease circulating VLDL levels, and because VLDL is the triglyceride-rich lipoprotein made by the liver, this helps reduce triglycerides by about 20-40%. This is a secondary lipid effect of HMG-CoA reductase inhibition.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Statins do not act on chylomicron formation in the enterocyte; ezetimibe acts at the intestinal level on cholesterol absorption.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Inhibiting adipose lipolysis is the action of niacin, not statins.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Blocking PCSK9-mediated LDL receptor degradation is the mechanism of PCSK9 inhibitors, not statins.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Lipoprotein lipase upregulation is the mechanism of fibrates and omega-3 fatty acids.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old woman with a low HDL cholesterol of 34 mg/dL asks whether the statin she was just prescribed will raise her HDL. Which of the following is the most accurate response regarding the effect of most statins on HDL levels?

explanation.summary: Most statins modestly increase HDL levels by about 5%.
explanation.whyCorrect: Statins primarily lower LDL-C by increasing hepatic LDL receptor expression, but they also modestly raise HDL, on the order of 5%. This is a small effect compared with their LDL-lowering action.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Statins increase rather than decrease HDL.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A 20-40% change describes the reduction in triglycerides from decreased VLDL, not the HDL effect.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A change greater than 50% describes the LDL-C lowering of a high-intensity statin, not the HDL effect.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Statins do produce a small, measurable rise in HDL.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old man with a myocardial infarction 2 years ago has a fasting LDL cholesterol of 105 mg/dL, which his previous physician described as acceptable. His new physician recommends starting a statin. Which of the following best justifies this recommendation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Benefit depends on raising HDL-C above a target threshold

choices.label: B
choices.text: Benefit is demonstrated only when LDL-C is markedly elevated

choices.label: C
choices.text: Benefit is limited to patients without established coronary disease

choices.label: D
choices.text: Statins repair myocardial tissue damaged by the prior infarction

choices.label: E
choices.text: Survival benefit is shown even when LDL-C is normal or borderline high

explanation.summary: Lipid lowering improves survival in both primary and secondary prevention, and the benefit has been shown even when cholesterol levels are 'normal' or borderline 'high.'
explanation.whyCorrect: This patient has established coronary disease, making this secondary prevention. Lipid lowering has been proven to improve survival in secondary prevention, and this benefit has been demonstrated when cholesterol levels are normal or only borderline high. Lowering lipid levels explains part of the benefit, but other factors such as plaque stabilization and reversal of endothelial dysfunction also play a role.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The HDL rise with statins is modest (about 5%) and is not the basis for the survival benefit.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The survival benefit has been shown at normal and borderline-high cholesterol levels, not only when LDL-C is markedly elevated.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Benefit is documented in both primary prevention (no clinical coronary disease) and secondary prevention (established coronary disease).
whyWrongByChoice.D: Statins stabilize plaque and reverse endothelial dysfunction; they do not repair infarcted myocardium.

questions.stem: A 61-year-old woman with carotid intimal thickening on ultrasound is started on a statin. She asks how soon regression of her atherosclerotic lesions might be expected. Based on reported studies, regression of atherosclerotic lesions with statin therapy has been observed within which of the following time frames?

choices.label: E
choices.text: Within 24 hours of the first dose

explanation.summary: Regression of atherosclerotic lesions with statins, seen as decreased thickness, has been reported within 12-24 months of therapy.
explanation.whyCorrect: Regression of atherosclerosis occurs with statin therapy, with a decrease in the thickness of lesions. The exact timing is not clear, but some studies have reported regression within 12-24 months of therapy.

whyWrongByChoice.A: One to two weeks is far shorter than the reported 12-24 month window for lesion regression.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Aminotransferase elevations may appear within the first three months, but plaque regression takes longer.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Four to six months is shorter than the 12-24 months reported in studies.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Structural regression of plaque does not occur within a day of starting therapy.

questions.stem: A 59-year-old man has a coronary plaque identified on imaging. His physician explains that statin therapy lowers his risk of an acute coronary syndrome caused by plaque rupture. Which of the following statin effects best accounts for this protection?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Increased degradation of hepatic LDL receptors

choices.label: B
choices.text: Increased hepatic secretion of VLDL particles

choices.label: C
choices.text: Maintenance of the integrity of the fibrous cap

choices.label: D
choices.text: Reversal of vasoconstriction in dysfunctional endothelium

choices.label: E
choices.text: Upregulation of PCSK9 on the hepatocyte surface

explanation.summary: Plaque stabilization by statins reflects lipid lowering helping to maintain the integrity of the fibrous cap, protecting against rupture.
explanation.whyCorrect: Coronary plaque rupture can lead to coronary syndromes. Lipid lowering with statins contributes to maintaining the integrity of the fibrous cap of the plaque, thereby protecting against rupture. This plaque-stabilizing effect is one of the non-lipid benefits that contribute to statins' cardiovascular protection.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Statins increase LDL receptor expression rather than degrading receptors.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Statins decrease circulating VLDL; increasing VLDL secretion would worsen dyslipidemia.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Reversal of endothelial dysfunction is a separate statin benefit that reduces vasoconstriction; it is not the mechanism protecting the fibrous cap from rupture.
whyWrongByChoice.E: PCSK9 promotes LDL receptor degradation; statins do not upregulate it as a therapeutic effect.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man is discharged after a myocardial infarction on atorvastatin 80 mg daily. According to AHA/ACC intensity classification, which of the following is the estimated LDL-C reduction expected with this regimen?

explanation.summary: Atorvastatin 40-80 mg is a high-intensity statin with an expected LDL-C lowering of more than 50%.
explanation.whyCorrect: High-intensity statins are defined by LDL-C lowering greater than 50% and include atorvastatin 40-80 mg and rosuvastatin 20-40 mg. Doses of atorvastatin above 40 mg are therefore high-intensity therapy.

whyWrongByChoice.A: About 5% is the modest HDL increase seen with statins, not the LDL-C effect of high-intensity therapy.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A 20-40% figure describes the triglyceride reduction from decreased VLDL, not the LDL-C reduction with atorvastatin 80 mg.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A 30-49% reduction defines moderate-intensity regimens such as atorvastatin 10-20 mg.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Less than 30% reduction defines low-intensity regimens such as simvastatin 10 mg.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old woman with a prior history of statin-associated muscle symptoms is to be restarted on the lowest-intensity statin regimen possible. Which of the following regimens is classified as low-intensity, with an expected LDL-C reduction of less than 30%?

explanation.summary: Simvastatin 10 mg is a low-intensity statin (LDL-C lowering less than 30%).
explanation.whyCorrect: Low-intensity regimens, defined by LDL-C lowering of less than 30%, include simvastatin 10 mg, pravastatin 10-20 mg, lovastatin 20 mg, and fluvastatin 20-40 mg.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Atorvastatin 10-20 mg is moderate-intensity (30-49% reduction).
whyWrongByChoice.B: Lovastatin 40-80 mg is moderate-intensity; only 20 mg is low-intensity.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Pravastatin 40-80 mg is moderate-intensity; only 10-20 mg is low-intensity.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Rosuvastatin 5-10 mg is moderate-intensity.

questions.stem: A 63-year-old man requires a moderate-intensity statin, defined as an expected LDL-C reduction of 30% to 49%. Which of the following regimens meets this definition?

explanation.summary: Fluvastatin XL 80 mg is a moderate-intensity regimen, even though fluvastatin 20-40 mg is low-intensity.
explanation.whyCorrect: Moderate-intensity regimens (30-49% LDL-C lowering) include atorvastatin 10-20 mg, rosuvastatin 5-10 mg, simvastatin 20-40 mg, pravastatin 40-80 mg, lovastatin 40-80 mg, and fluvastatin XL 80 mg. Fluvastatin therefore spans two categories depending on dose.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Lovastatin 20 mg is low-intensity; 40-80 mg would be moderate.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Pravastatin 10-20 mg is low-intensity; 40-80 mg would be moderate.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Rosuvastatin 20-40 mg is high-intensity (more than 50% reduction).
whyWrongByChoice.E: Simvastatin 10 mg is low-intensity; 20-40 mg would be moderate.

questions.stem: A pharmacology student notes that all statins are given orally yet have low systemic bioavailability. Which of the following best explains this pharmacokinetic property?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Binding to bile acids within the intestinal lumen

choices.label: B
choices.text: Degradation by gastric acid before absorption

choices.label: C
choices.text: Extensive first-pass metabolism by the liver

choices.label: D
choices.text: Poor dissolution of the tablets in the intestinal lumen

choices.label: E
choices.text: Rapid unchanged excretion by the kidneys

explanation.summary: Statins have low systemic bioavailability because they undergo extensive first-pass metabolism by the liver.
explanation.whyCorrect: All statins are taken orally and undergo extensive hepatic first-pass metabolism, which is why their systemic bioavailability is low and why monitoring liver function is important during statin therapy.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Bile acid binding is the mechanism of bile acid resins, not a property of statins.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Gastric degradation is not the explanation offered for the low bioavailability of statins.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Low bioavailability of statins is attributed to hepatic first-pass metabolism, not tablet dissolution.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Statins are cleared by hepatic metabolism or hepatic transporters rather than rapid renal excretion of unchanged drug.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man started on atorvastatin 80 mg daily 6 weeks ago is found on routine laboratory testing to have a mild elevation in serum aminotransferases. Which of the following best characterizes statin-associated aminotransferase elevation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Appears only after several years of continuous statin therapy

choices.label: B
choices.text: Idiosyncratic and entirely unrelated to the dose administered

choices.label: C
choices.text: Occurs exclusively with the hydrophilic statins such as pravastatin

choices.label: D
choices.text: Requires a concurrent CYP3A4 inhibitor such as clarithromycin to develop

choices.label: E
choices.text: Typically occurs within the first three months and is dose-dependent

explanation.summary: Statin-induced aminotransferase elevations occur within the first three months of therapy and are dose-dependent.
explanation.whyCorrect: Statins can elevate liver aminotransferases within the first three months of therapy, and the effect is dose-dependent. This patient on a high-intensity dose at 6 weeks fits the expected pattern, which is why liver function is monitored with statin use.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Aminotransferase elevations appear early, within the first three months, not after years of therapy.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The hepatic effect is dose-dependent rather than idiosyncratic.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hepatic dysfunction is a class effect and is not limited to hydrophilic statins.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Aminotransferase elevation can occur from the statin alone; a CYP3A4 inhibitor is not required.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old woman taking simvastatin has an asymptomatic serum ALT that is 3.5 times the upper limit of normal on a single laboratory measurement. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Add ezetimibe and halve the simvastatin dose without repeat testing

choices.label: B
choices.text: Continue simvastatin unchanged and recheck the ALT in one year

choices.label: C
choices.text: Discontinue simvastatin now and start a fibrate in its place

choices.label: D
choices.text: Repeat the ALT to confirm the elevation before discontinuing

choices.label: E
choices.text: Switch to atorvastatin at an equivalent statin intensity today

explanation.summary: Discontinuation or an alternate agent is recommended for ALT greater than three times the upper limit only when confirmed by a second laboratory test.
explanation.whyCorrect: Statin discontinuation or the use of alternate agents is recommended in patients with ALT levels three times the upper limit that are confirmed by a second lab test. A single elevated value should therefore be confirmed before the drug is stopped.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Adding ezetimibe does not address the need to confirm a significant aminotransferase elevation.
whyWrongByChoice.B: An ALT above three times the upper limit warrants confirmation now, not continuing unchanged for a year.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Discontinuation is recommended only after the elevation is confirmed on a second test.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Atorvastatin is also extensively hepatically metabolized; switching before confirming the elevation is not the recommended step.

questions.stem: A 64-year-old man taking atorvastatin reports difficulty climbing stairs and rising from a chair for 3 weeks. Examination shows proximal muscle weakness. Serum creatine phosphokinase is mildly elevated, urinalysis is negative for myoglobin, and serum creatinine is normal. Which of the following statin-associated muscle symptom categories best describes his presentation?

explanation.summary: Statin-associated myopathy is muscle weakness with or without CPK elevation.
explanation.whyCorrect: SAMS spans myalgia (aches, soreness, tenderness, or cramps), myopathy (muscle weakness with or without CPK elevations), myositis (inflammation), and clinical rhabdomyolysis (significantly elevated CPK with myoglobinuria and acute kidney injury). Weakness with a mild CPK rise, no myoglobinuria, and normal renal function fits myopathy.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Hepatic dysfunction manifests as elevated aminotransferases, not muscle weakness.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Myalgia describes muscle aches, soreness, tenderness, or cramps without the weakness that dominates this presentation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Myositis denotes muscle inflammation; the presentation here is defined by weakness with a mild CPK rise.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Rhabdomyolysis requires significantly elevated CPK with myoglobinuria and acute kidney injury, which are absent.

questions.stem: A 67-year-old man develops muscle pain on lovastatin, and his physician switches him to fluvastatin, noting it carries the lowest risk of myopathy. Which of the following best explains why fluvastatin has a lower myopathy risk than lovastatin?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Fluvastatin has a longer elimination half-life

choices.label: D
choices.text: Fluvastatin is not metabolized by CYP3A4

explanation.summary: Fluvastatin, pravastatin, and pitavastatin have the lowest myopathy risk because they are not CYP3A4 metabolized.
explanation.whyCorrect: The risk of myopathy is lowest with fluvastatin, pravastatin, and pitavastatin since they are not metabolized by CYP3A4, whereas lovastatin, simvastatin, and atorvastatin (CYP3A4 substrates) carry a higher SAMS risk. Fluvastatin clearance is instead partly dependent on CYP2C9.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Fluvastatin has a short half-life (about 0.5-2.3 hours), which is why it is taken in the evening.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Fluvastatin is a low-intensity (20-40 mg) or moderate-intensity (XL 80 mg) statin, not high-intensity.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Fluvastatin is lipophilic; the hydrophilic statins are pravastatin and rosuvastatin.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Minimal hepatic metabolism describes pitavastatin; fluvastatin is metabolized by hepatic CYP2C9.

questions.stem: A 57-year-old man has been taking simvastatin 40 mg daily for 6 months. His LDL cholesterol remains well above goal. His physician wants to achieve a greater than 50% LDL-C reduction. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Add a second 40 mg dose of simvastatin in the morning

choices.label: B
choices.text: Continue simvastatin 40 mg and repeat the lipid panel in one year

explanation.summary: Simvastatin is capped at 40 mg/day to prevent SAMS, so a high-intensity goal requires switching to atorvastatin 40-80 mg or rosuvastatin 20-40 mg.
explanation.whyCorrect: The simvastatin dose is maxed at 40 mg/day to prevent statin-associated muscle symptoms, and simvastatin 20-40 mg is only moderate-intensity (30-49% reduction). Achieving more than 50% LDL-C reduction therefore requires a high-intensity regimen such as atorvastatin 40-80 mg or rosuvastatin 20-40 mg.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Adding a second dose brings the total to 80 mg/day, exceeding the maximum.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Continuing an inadequate regimen for another year does not address the LDL-C goal.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Simvastatin 60 mg also exceeds the 40 mg/day maximum.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Simvastatin 80 mg exceeds the 40 mg/day maximum set to prevent SAMS.

questions.stem: A 48-year-old woman on simvastatin reports diffuse muscle aches for 2 months. She also notes fatigue, weight gain, and cold intolerance. Which of the following laboratory tests is most likely to identify a condition that predisposes her to statin-associated muscle symptoms?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Fasting lipid panel with LDL cholesterol

choices.label: B
choices.text: Fasting plasma glucose and hemoglobin A1c

explanation.summary: Hypothyroidism predisposes patients to statin-associated muscle symptoms.
explanation.whyCorrect: Hypothyroidism can predispose patients to SAMS. This woman's fatigue, weight gain, and cold intolerance suggest hypothyroidism, so a TSH would identify the predisposing condition. Low vitamin D is another factor associated with high rates of myalgia and myopathy.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A lipid panel assesses efficacy, not a predisposition to muscle symptoms.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Glucose relates to the statin-associated diabetes risk, not to SAMS predisposition.
whyWrongByChoice.C: ALT screens for statin hepatic dysfunction, not a predisposition to muscle symptoms.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Creatinine assesses for acute kidney injury in rhabdomyolysis but does not identify a predisposing condition.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old woman who rarely goes outdoors develops myalgias after starting a statin. Low levels of which of the following are associated with high rates of statin-associated myalgia and myopathy?

explanation.summary: Low vitamin D levels are associated with high rates of statin-associated myalgia and myopathy.
explanation.whyCorrect: Along with hypothyroidism, low vitamin D is a recognized factor associated with high rates of myalgia and myopathy in patients taking statins.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Folate deficiency is not described as predisposing to SAMS.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Iron deficiency is not associated with statin muscle symptoms.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Vitamin B12 deficiency is not the factor linked to statin muscle symptoms.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Vitamin K is not associated with statin-associated myalgia or myopathy.

questions.stem: A 33-year-old woman with hypercholesterolemia stopped her statin when she became pregnant. She has just delivered and plans to breastfeed for 6 months. She asks whether she can restart her statin now. Which of the following is the most appropriate advice?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Breastfeeding is not recommended while taking a statin

choices.label: B
choices.text: Restart at half the previous dose during lactation

choices.label: C
choices.text: Restart only a hydrophilic statin while breastfeeding

choices.label: D
choices.text: Restart the statin; it is compatible with breastfeeding

choices.label: E
choices.text: Take the statin immediately after each feeding

explanation.summary: Breastfeeding is not recommended in patients taking a statin.
explanation.whyCorrect: Statins should be discontinued in pregnant patients, and breastfeeding is not recommended in patients taking a statin. She should not combine statin therapy with breastfeeding.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Dose reduction does not change the recommendation against breastfeeding on a statin.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The recommendation against breastfeeding applies to statins as a class, not only lipophilic agents.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Statins are not considered compatible with breastfeeding.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Timing the dose around feedings does not make statin use acceptable during breastfeeding.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old man on rosuvastatin is hospitalized and started on intravenous daptomycin for a bloodstream infection. One week later he develops muscle pain, and his creatine phosphokinase is markedly elevated. Which of the following best explains this finding?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Daptomycin converts rosuvastatin to a lipophilic form

choices.label: B
choices.text: Daptomycin decreases renal clearance of rosuvastatin

choices.label: C
choices.text: Daptomycin displaces rosuvastatin from plasma proteins

choices.label: D
choices.text: Daptomycin independently raises myopathy risk and CPK levels

choices.label: E
choices.text: Daptomycin inhibits CYP3A4 metabolism of rosuvastatin

explanation.summary: Daptomycin and glucocorticoids increase the risk of myopathy and can raise CPK levels when used with statins, independent of CYP metabolism.
explanation.whyCorrect: Drugs such as glucocorticoids and daptomycin also increase the risk of myopathy and can increase CPK levels with statin use. This is an additive muscle toxicity rather than a pharmacokinetic interaction, which is why it occurs even with rosuvastatin, a statin cleared by non-CYP450 (OATP transporter) pathways.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Daptomycin does not change the solubility properties of rosuvastatin, which is hydrophilic.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The interaction is not explained by altered renal clearance of the statin.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Protein-binding displacement is not the mechanism described for daptomycin's effect on statin myopathy.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Rosuvastatin is cleared primarily by non-CYP450 transformations, so CYP3A4 inhibition does not explain this interaction.

questions.stem: A 69-year-old woman with hypertension controlled on amlodipine develops muscle aches 3 weeks after starting atorvastatin. Her physician attributes the symptoms to a pharmacokinetic drug interaction. Which of the following changes is most appropriate to eliminate this interaction while continuing lipid-lowering therapy?

explanation.summary: Calcium channel blockers moderately inhibit CYP3A4; switching to a statin cleared by non-CYP450 pathways (rosuvastatin) removes the interaction.
explanation.whyCorrect: Amlodipine, diltiazem, and verapamil are moderate inhibitors of CYP3A4 metabolism and can increase adverse drug reactions in statins metabolized by CYP3A4, such as atorvastatin. Rosuvastatin is cleared primarily by non-CYP450 (OATP transporter) transformations, so switching to it eliminates the CYP3A4-based interaction.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Diltiazem is likewise a moderate CYP3A4 inhibitor and would not resolve the interaction.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Verapamil is also a moderate CYP3A4 inhibitor, so the interaction with atorvastatin would persist.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Lovastatin is metabolized by CYP3A4 and would still interact with amlodipine.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Simvastatin is metabolized by CYP3A4 and would still interact with amlodipine.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman of Asian ancestry with hypercholesterolemia is to begin rosuvastatin. Based on genetic differences in drug metabolism, which of the following is recommended when initiating her therapy?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Administer the drug only in the evening

choices.label: B
choices.text: Begin with a lower initial dose

choices.label: C
choices.text: Obtain a baseline creatine phosphokinase level

choices.label: D
choices.text: Start at the standard high-intensity dose

explanation.summary: A lower initial dose of rosuvastatin is recommended in Asian individuals because of genetic differences in the rate of drug metabolism.
explanation.whyCorrect: Genetics plays a role in the variability of statin response and side effects, in part through differences in the rate of drug metabolism. As an example, a lower initial dose of rosuvastatin is recommended in Asian individuals.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Rosuvastatin has a long half-life (about 19 hours) and can be taken at any time of day.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A baseline CPK is not the genetics-based recommendation for initiating rosuvastatin.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Starting at a standard high dose ignores the recommendation for a lower initial dose in Asian patients.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Simvastatin's tolerability is itself influenced by CYP2D6 phenotype and is not the recommended substitution.

questions.stem: A 54-year-old man started on a statin 2 weeks ago reports loose stools several times a day but has no muscle pain, weakness, or jaundice. Which of the following is the most likely explanation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A common gastrointestinal adverse effect of statins

choices.label: B
choices.text: Bile acid malabsorption caused by the statin in the ileum

choices.label: C
choices.text: Statin-associated muscle symptoms from myocyte injury

choices.label: E
choices.text: Statin-induced loss of glycemic control with hyperglycemia

explanation.summary: Diarrhea is a common gastrointestinal adverse effect of the statin class.
explanation.whyCorrect: Among statin adverse effects, diarrhea is described as a common gastrointestinal effect of the drug class. In the absence of muscle symptoms or hepatic findings, the loose stools are best attributed to this GI effect.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Statins do not act on intestinal bile acid handling; that is the domain of bile acid resins.
whyWrongByChoice.C: SAMS involves muscle aches, weakness, or CPK elevation, none of which are present.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Hepatic dysfunction presents with elevated aminotransferases, and the patient has no jaundice or hepatic findings.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Loss of glycemic control is a metabolic effect on beta-cells and does not present as diarrhea.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man who smokes three-quarters of a pack of cigarettes daily and has a BMI of 27 kg/m2 is found to have an LDL cholesterol of 200 mg/dL and HDL cholesterol of 32 mg/dL. He is prescribed atorvastatin. Which of the following counseling points about his medication is correct?

choices.label: B
choices.text: It can be taken at any time of the day

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is cleared mainly by a hepatic OATP transporter

choices.label: D
choices.text: It must be taken in the evening to be effective

choices.label: E
choices.text: Its short half-life requires twice-daily dosing

explanation.summary: Atorvastatin has a long half-life (about 15-30 hours) and can be taken at any time of day, but grapefruit juice should be avoided.
explanation.whyCorrect: Atorvastatin's long elimination half-life means it can be administered at any time of the day, unlike simvastatin and lovastatin, which should be taken in the evening. The longer half-life also contributes to its stronger cholesterol-lowering effect. Because atorvastatin is metabolized by CYP3A4, the patient should avoid grapefruit juice, which inhibits intestinal CYP3A4.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Grapefruit juice inhibits intestinal CYP3A4 and raises levels of CYP3A4-metabolized statins; it should be avoided.
whyWrongByChoice.C: OATP transporter clearance describes pravastatin and rosuvastatin; atorvastatin is metabolized by hepatic CYP3A4.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Evening administration is the counseling pearl for short half-life statins such as simvastatin and lovastatin, not atorvastatin.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Atorvastatin has a long half-life of about 15-30 hours and does not require twice-daily dosing.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old man of European ancestry has had a smaller-than-expected LDL-C reduction and poor tolerability on simvastatin. His physician suspects a genetic difference in drug metabolism. A functionally absent phenotype of which of the following enzymes is reported to affect both the lipid-lowering response and tolerability of simvastatin?

explanation.summary: CYP2D6 phenotype affects both the degree of lipid lowering and the tolerability of simvastatin.
explanation.whyCorrect: CYP2D6 phenotype appears to be important in patients treated with simvastatin, as it can affect both the degree of lipid lowering and tolerability. CYP2D6 is functionally absent in about 7 percent of White and African American individuals, while deficiency is rare among Asian persons.

whyWrongByChoice.A: CYP2C9 partly governs fluvastatin clearance and is not the phenotype linked to simvastatin response variability.
whyWrongByChoice.C: CYP3A4 metabolizes simvastatin and is the target of drug interactions, but the phenotype linked to variable response and tolerability is CYP2D6.
whyWrongByChoice.D: HMG-CoA reductase is the drug target, not a metabolizing enzyme with a described absent phenotype.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Lipoprotein lipase is the target of fibrates and is unrelated to simvastatin metabolism.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old man with stable angina takes a sublingual nitroglycerin tablet during an episode of exertional chest pain, and his symptoms resolve within minutes. Which of the following best describes the primary mechanism by which this drug relieves his chest pain?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It antagonizes beta-adrenergic receptors on the myocardium

choices.label: B
choices.text: It blocks L-type calcium channels in vascular smooth muscle

choices.label: C
choices.text: It increases heart rate and contractility to improve perfusion

choices.label: D
choices.text: It inhibits platelet aggregation within the coronary arteries

choices.label: E
choices.text: It is converted to nitric oxide

explanation.summary: Nitrates are converted to nitric oxide, which activates guanylyl cyclase and raises cGMP to relax vascular smooth muscle.
explanation.whyCorrect: In the body, nitrates are converted to nitric oxide (NO). NO activates guanylyl cyclase, which increases cGMP and causes relaxation (dilation) of vascular smooth muscle. This vasodilation is the basis for the anti-anginal effect of nitrates.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Beta-blockade is not the mechanism of nitrates and is not described in the brick.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Calcium-channel blockade is the mechanism of a different drug class; nitrates act through the NO/cGMP pathway.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Nitrates reduce cardiac workload; they do not primarily increase heart rate and contractility.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The brick attributes the anti-anginal effect to vasodilation, not to antiplatelet action.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old woman is treated with nitroglycerin for angina. The drug reduces her myocardial oxygen demand. Which of the following effects most directly accounts for this reduction in oxygen demand?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A reflex increase in myocardial contraction force

choices.label: B
choices.text: An increase in heart rate to improve tissue perfusion

choices.label: C
choices.text: An increase in systemic vascular resistance

choices.label: E
choices.text: Dilation of the large veins returning to the heart

explanation.summary: Nitrate-induced venodilation lowers the work of the heart and reduces myocardial oxygen use.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that relaxation (dilation) of the large veins that return to the heart decreases contraction force, increases blood flow, and reduces myocardial oxygen use. Lowering the workload of the heart in this way decreases its oxygen demand and relieves ischemic chest pain.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Nitrates decrease contraction force; they do not reflexively increase it.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Increasing heart rate would raise, not lower, myocardial oxygen demand.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Nitrates cause vasodilation and lower vascular resistance rather than increasing it.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Nitrates dilate coronary arteries; they do not constrict them.

questions.stem: In addition to reducing the heart's oxygen demand, nitrates relieve angina through an effect that increases oxygen supply to the myocardium. Which of the following best describes this additional effect?

choices.label: A
choices.text: An increase in blood hemoglobin concentration

choices.label: B
choices.text: Constriction of peripheral veins to raise coronary perfusion pressure

choices.label: D
choices.text: Dissolution of atherosclerotic plaque within the coronary arteries

choices.label: E
choices.text: Stimulation of new coronary vessel growth

explanation.summary: Nitrates also cause direct coronary artery vasodilation, increasing oxygen supply to the heart.
explanation.whyCorrect: Beyond lowering oxygen demand through venodilation, the brick notes that nitrates cause some direct coronary artery vasodilation that increases oxygen supply to the heart, further relieving chest pain.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Nitrates do not raise hemoglobin concentration.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Nitrates dilate veins rather than constricting them, and venoconstriction is not their mechanism.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Nitrates relieve symptoms by vasodilation; they do not dissolve plaque.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Nitrates act acutely by dilating existing vessels, not by growing new ones.

questions.stem: A 67-year-old man develops acute substernal chest pain in the emergency department. He is given a nitroglycerin tablet to place under his tongue. Which of the following best explains why the sublingual route is preferred for acute angina?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It automatically provides a built-in nitrate-free interval

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is effective only for chronic angina, not acute episodes

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is rapidly absorbed and avoids first-pass hepatic metabolism

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is slowly absorbed, providing sustained drug levels over many hours

choices.label: E
choices.text: It undergoes extensive first-pass metabolism before reaching the circulation

explanation.summary: Sublingual nitroglycerin is absorbed rapidly and bypasses first-pass metabolism, giving fast relief of acute angina.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that sublingual nitroglycerin tablets are the most common form: placed under the tongue, they avoid first-pass metabolism, are rapidly absorbed, and can quickly relieve angina. This makes them ideal for acute episodes.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A nitrate-free interval is a deliberate dosing strategy, not an inherent feature of a single sublingual tablet.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Sublingual nitroglycerin is a short-acting agent used for acute angina.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Slow, sustained absorption describes oral agents like isosorbide mononitrate, not sublingual nitroglycerin.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Avoiding first-pass metabolism is precisely the advantage of the sublingual route.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man with chronic stable angina is prescribed a nitrate that is swallowed as an oral tablet, is slowly absorbed, and undergoes first-pass metabolism. Which of the following agents is he most likely taking?

explanation.summary: Oral isosorbide mononitrate is slowly absorbed, undergoes first-pass metabolism, and is used for chronic angina.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick describes isosorbide mononitrate as a delayed-release tablet that is swallowed, slowly absorbed, and undergoes first-pass metabolism. Despite this, it produces the same vasodilation effects and is used for chronic angina.

whyWrongByChoice.A: IV nitroglycerin is given intravenously and bypasses first-pass metabolism, and it is short-acting for acute use.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Sodium nitroprusside is an IV short-acting agent, not an oral tablet.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Sublingual nitroglycerin is placed under the tongue and avoids first-pass metabolism.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Translingual nitroglycerin is a spray applied to the tongue and is short-acting for acute angina.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman with severe chest pain has received repeated doses of sublingual nitroglycerin, but her pain keeps returning after each dose wears off. The physician applies a transdermal nitroglycerin patch to her chest. Which property of the patch makes it useful in this situation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It avoids all systemic absorption, acting only locally on the skin

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is indicated exclusively for chronic angina and never for acute pain

choices.label: C
choices.text: It works by a mechanism unrelated to nitric oxide

choices.label: D
choices.text: Its delayed onset and slower absorption through the skin

choices.label: E
choices.text: Its immediate onset makes it faster than sublingual tablets

explanation.summary: Transdermal nitroglycerin has a delayed onset and is more slowly absorbed, giving a continuous effect useful for persistent, late acute angina.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick explains that nitroglycerin ointment and the transdermal patch have a delayed onset because of transdermal absorption. This makes them useful for late acute angina: rather than repeatedly re-dosing sublingual nitroglycerin, applying a patch provides a continuous effect as the drug is more slowly absorbed.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The patch is absorbed transdermally into the circulation to produce systemic vasodilation.
whyWrongByChoice.B: In this clinical scenario the patch is used for continuing (late) acute angina, not only chronic angina.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Like all nitrates, the patch works through conversion to nitric oxide.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The patch has a delayed, not immediate, onset; sublingual tablets act faster.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man is started on nitroglycerin for angina. Which of the following is the most common adverse effect he is likely to experience?

explanation.summary: Headache is the most common adverse effect of nitrates.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that the most common adverse effect of nitrates is headache, reported by more than 60% of patients who receive nitroglycerin. It is thought to result from the rapid vasodilation nitroglycerin produces, and is notably less common with long-acting isosorbide mononitrate.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Bradycardia is not described as a nitrate adverse effect in the brick.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Constipation is not a nitrate adverse effect discussed in the brick.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Dry cough is associated with a different drug class, not nitrates.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Nitrates cause vasodilation and hypotension, not hypertension.

questions.stem: A 65-year-old man with a history of atherosclerosis develops chest pain when he walks uphill. His physician explains that his angina pectoris is caused by which of the following underlying processes?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Excess oxygen supply to the myocardium

choices.label: D
choices.text: Obstruction of a pulmonary artery by a thrombus

choices.label: E
choices.text: Spasm of the lower esophageal sphincter

explanation.summary: Angina pectoris is chest pain caused by myocardial ischemia, a lack of oxygen reaching heart cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick defines angina pectoris as chest pain caused by myocardial ischemia (lack of oxygen leading toward cardiac cell death). Atherosclerosis reduces the effective diameter of blood vessels, lowering blood flow and oxygen delivery to the myocardium and producing the ischemic chest pain.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Angina results from insufficient, not excess, oxygen delivery to the heart.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Pericardial inflammation is a different entity and is not the cause of angina described here.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Pulmonary embolism is a separate condition and is not the described cause of angina.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Esophageal spasm can mimic chest pain but is not the mechanism of angina pectoris.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old man is receiving intravenous nitroglycerin. Which of the following adverse effects most specifically requires that his blood pressure be monitored regularly during this therapy?

explanation.summary: IV nitrates cause significant vasodilation that can produce hypotension, so blood pressure must be monitored regularly.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick notes that IV nitroglycerin and sodium nitroprusside are used to acutely lower blood pressure, and the significant vasodilation they cause can produce hypotension. Any patient receiving nitrates should have blood pressure monitored regularly.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Headache is the most common adverse effect but is not the reason blood pressure is monitored.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Nitrate tolerance is a loss of drug effect over time, not an indication for blood-pressure monitoring.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Peripheral edema is not a nitrate adverse effect discussed in the brick.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Reflex bradycardia is not the monitored concern described in the brick.

questions.stem: A 65-year-old man whose angina is usually well controlled has now received continuous nitrate therapy for more than 14 hours without any nitrate-free period. His previously controlled chest pain has returned despite ongoing dosing. Which of the following best explains the loss of drug efficacy?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A paradoxical reflex vasoconstriction caused by cGMP

choices.label: B
choices.text: An IgE-mediated allergic reaction to nitrates

choices.label: C
choices.text: Enhanced conversion of nitroglycerin to nitric oxide

choices.label: D
choices.text: Increased first-pass metabolism raising active drug levels

choices.label: E
choices.text: Nitrate tolerance from sustained high-dose exposure

explanation.summary: Continuous exposure to high-dose nitrates causes tolerance (tachyphylaxis), attenuating their effect.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick teaches that frequently repeated or continuous exposure to high doses of nitrates leads to tolerance (tachyphylaxis), a marked attenuation of most of their pharmacological effects. After more than 14 hours of continuous nitrates without a nitrate-free interval, the returning chest pain reflects developing nitrate tolerance.

whyWrongByChoice.A: cGMP mediates vasodilation; a paradoxical reflex vasoconstriction from cGMP is not described.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The brick attributes the loss of effect to tolerance, not to an allergic (IgE-mediated) reaction.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Tolerance is associated with reduced, not enhanced, conversion of nitroglycerin to NO.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Increased active drug levels would enhance, not reduce, the effect.

questions.stem: A physician wants to design a nitrate regimen that minimizes the development of tolerance in a patient on long-acting nitrate therapy. Which of the following strategies is most appropriate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Administer the nitrate continuously without interruption

choices.label: B
choices.text: Give the drug every 4 hours without any break

choices.label: C
choices.text: Include a daily 10-12 hour nitrate-free interval

choices.label: D
choices.text: Steadily increase the dose over time

choices.label: E
choices.text: Switch the patient to intravenous dosing around the clock

explanation.summary: A daily 10-12 hour nitrate-free interval decreases the likelihood of nitrate tolerance.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that nitrate therapy should be designed to prevent tolerance, and that nitrates require a 10-12 hour nitrate-free interval to decrease the likelihood of tolerance and allow the return of efficacy. For example, a patch is worn for 12-14 hours and removed for 10-12 hours.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Continuous, uninterrupted dosing promotes tolerance rather than preventing it.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Frequent dosing with no break provides continuous exposure, promoting tolerance.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Increasing the dose does not prevent tolerance and can worsen adverse effects.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Around-the-clock IV dosing provides no nitrate-free interval and would encourage tolerance.

questions.stem: A pharmacology student is asked to describe a proposed cellular mechanism underlying nitrate tolerance. Which of the following best fits what the brick describes?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A reduced capacity to convert nitroglycerin to nitric oxide

choices.label: B
choices.text: An increase in intracellular cGMP production

choices.label: C
choices.text: Downregulation of beta-adrenergic receptors in the myocardium

choices.label: D
choices.text: Enhanced first-pass metabolism that increases active drug delivery

choices.label: E
choices.text: Upregulation of guanylyl cyclase in vascular smooth muscle

explanation.summary: Nitrate tolerance may result from reduced ability of vascular smooth muscle to convert nitroglycerin to NO.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that the magnitude of tolerance is a function of dosage and frequency of use, and that tolerance may result from a reduced capacity of the vascular smooth muscle to convert nitroglycerin to NO (true vascular tolerance) or from activation of mechanisms extraneous to the vessel wall.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Increased cGMP would strengthen the response, the opposite of tolerance.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Beta-receptor downregulation is unrelated to the nitrate NO/cGMP mechanism.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Tolerance is a pharmacodynamic loss of effect at the vessel, not increased active drug delivery.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Tolerance reflects a diminished vasodilatory response; upregulating guanylyl cyclase would enhance, not blunt, the effect.

questions.stem: A 59-year-old man takes a sublingual nitroglycerin tablet for exertional chest pain. After the drug is converted to nitric oxide in the body, which of the following enzymes is directly activated to initiate relaxation of vascular smooth muscle?

explanation.summary: Nitric oxide activates guanylyl cyclase in vascular smooth muscle.
explanation.whyCorrect: Nitrates are converted to nitric oxide (NO), which activates guanylyl cyclase. Guanylyl cyclase then generates cGMP, and the rise in cGMP produces relaxation (dilation) of vascular smooth muscle, the basis of the anti-anginal effect.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Adenylyl cyclase generates cAMP; the nitrate pathway shown in the brick runs through guanylyl cyclase and cGMP.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Phosphodiesterase degrades cyclic nucleotides; it is not activated by NO to cause relaxation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Phospholipase C is not the enzyme NO activates in this pathway.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Protein kinase A is a cAMP-dependent kinase and is not the enzyme NO directly activates.

questions.stem: A pharmacology student traces the signaling pathway by which nitroglycerin relaxes vascular smooth muscle. After guanylyl cyclase is activated, which of the following molecules serves as the substrate from which the vasodilatory second messenger is produced?

explanation.summary: Guanylyl cyclase converts GTP to cGMP, the second messenger that relaxes vascular smooth muscle.
explanation.whyCorrect: In the pathway the brick depicts, NO activates guanylyl cyclase, which converts GTP into cGMP. The increase in cGMP within the vascular smooth muscle cell produces relaxation and vasodilation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: ATP is the substrate for adenylyl cyclase producing cAMP, not for guanylyl cyclase.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Calcium is an ion involved in contraction; it is not the substrate of guanylyl cyclase.
whyWrongByChoice.C: cAMP is a different second messenger and is not the product of guanylyl cyclase.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Inositol trisphosphate is a product of phospholipase C signaling, not of guanylyl cyclase.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old woman has predictable chest pain with exertion that has been unchanged for two years. In the context of nitrate treatment, her physician refers to her condition as "chronic" angina. Which of the following types of angina is being described?

explanation.summary: When discussing nitrate treatment, stable angina is referred to as "chronic" and unstable angina as "acute."
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick identifies three types of angina: stable, unstable, and vasospastic. In the context of nitrate treatment it refers to unstable angina as "acute" and stable angina as "chronic," a distinction that affects which route of administration is chosen.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Acute coronary syndrome encompasses unstable angina and myocardial infarction; it is not the "chronic" designation.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Myocardial infarction is a separate form of ischemic heart disease, not a type of angina.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Unstable angina is what the brick calls "acute" angina, not "chronic."
whyWrongByChoice.E: Vasospastic angina is the third type listed but is not the entity the brick labels "chronic."

questions.stem: A cardiology fellow reviews the classification of ischemic heart disease. Which of the following conditions falls under ischemic heart disease but is NOT categorized as part of acute coronary syndrome?

explanation.summary: Stable angina is a form of ischemic heart disease that sits outside acute coronary syndrome.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick's figure divides ischemic heart disease into acute coronary syndrome (which includes myocardial infarction and unstable angina) and stable angina, which branches directly from ischemic heart disease without being part of acute coronary syndrome.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Myocardial infarction is shown as a component of acute coronary syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Pericarditis is not a form of ischemic heart disease in the brick's classification.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Pulmonary embolism is not part of ischemic heart disease.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Unstable angina is shown as a component of acute coronary syndrome.

questions.stem: A 71-year-old man with stable angina is to be started on a nitrate for daily prevention of chest pain rather than for aborting an acute attack. Which of the following agents has a delayed onset of action and is used for chronic angina?

explanation.summary: Isosorbide dinitrate is a long-acting, delayed-onset nitrate used for chronic angina.
explanation.whyCorrect: In the brick's categorization table, isosorbide dinitrate is listed alongside isosorbide mononitrate as a long-acting nitrate with delayed onset that is used for chronic angina.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Intravenous nitroglycerin is short-acting with short onset, used for acute angina.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Sodium nitroprusside is an IV short-acting agent used for acute angina, not for chronic prevention.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The sublingual nitroglycerin tablet is short-acting with short onset, used for acute angina.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Translingual nitroglycerin spray is a short-acting agent with short onset, used for acute angina.

questions.stem: A 63-year-old man with a dry mouth has difficulty dissolving tablets under his tongue, so his physician prescribes a nitroglycerin spray applied to the tongue for use during chest pain episodes. How is this translingual formulation categorized?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Delayed onset; used for chronic angina

explanation.summary: Translingual nitroglycerin spray is a short-acting, short-onset nitrate for acute angina.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick's table lists translingual nitroglycerin (spray) among the short-acting nitrates, with a short onset time and use for acute angina, alongside the sublingual tablet, IV nitroglycerin, and IV sodium nitroprusside.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The spray has a short, not delayed, onset.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The long-acting agents used for acute angina are nitroglycerin ointment and the transdermal patch, which have delayed onset.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Long-acting agents for chronic angina are the isosorbide preparations, not the spray.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Short-acting nitrates in the brick are all used for acute angina, not chronic.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man in the intensive care unit is receiving an intravenous nitrate with a short onset that is categorized for acute use, but the agent is not nitroglycerin. Which of the following is he most likely receiving?

explanation.summary: Sodium nitroprusside is an IV, short-acting, short-onset nitrate used acutely.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick's table lists sodium nitroprusside (IV) among the short-acting nitrates with short onset used for acute angina. It is also mentioned, together with IV nitroglycerin, as a nitrate used to acutely lower blood pressure.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Isosorbide dinitrate is a delayed-onset, long-acting agent for chronic angina, not an IV drug.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Isosorbide mononitrate is an oral, delayed-onset, long-acting agent for chronic angina.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Nitroglycerin ointment is applied to the skin and has a delayed onset.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The transdermal patch is applied to the skin and has a delayed onset; it is not given IV.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old woman in the emergency department has recurrent chest pain that keeps returning after each dose of sublingual nitroglycerin wears off. The physician chooses a long-acting nitrate that is nonetheless categorized for acute angina. Which of the following agents fits this description?

explanation.summary: Nitroglycerin ointment is a long-acting nitrate with delayed onset that is used for "late" acute angina.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick's table marks nitroglycerin ointment and the transdermal patch as long-acting nitrates with delayed onset that are used for acute angina (asterisked). Its clinical correlation explains that, rather than repeatedly re-dosing sublingual nitroglycerin, ointment or a patch can be applied to the chest to provide a continuous effect as the drug is slowly absorbed.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Intravenous nitroglycerin is a short-acting agent with short onset.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Isosorbide dinitrate is long-acting but is used for chronic angina.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Isosorbide mononitrate is long-acting but is used only for chronic angina.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The translingual spray is a short-acting agent, not a long-acting one.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man who had severe headaches with sublingual nitroglycerin reports far fewer headaches after being switched to daily isosorbide mononitrate. Which of the following best explains the difference?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Isosorbide mononitrate acts only on the coronary arteries, not veins

choices.label: C
choices.text: Isosorbide mononitrate constricts rather than dilates cerebral vessels

choices.label: D
choices.text: Isosorbide mononitrate is absorbed slowly, without rapid vasodilation

choices.label: E
choices.text: Isosorbide mononitrate is never converted to nitric oxide in the body

explanation.summary: Headache from nitrates is attributed to rapid vasodilation, which is less pronounced with slowly absorbed long-acting isosorbide mononitrate.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that headache likely occurs because of the rapid vasodilation that occurs with nitroglycerin, and that the headache rate is significantly lower in patients taking long-acting isosorbide mononitrate. Isosorbide mononitrate is a delayed-release tablet that is slowly absorbed, so it does not produce the abrupt vasodilation of sublingual nitroglycerin.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Isosorbide mononitrate causes the same systemic vasodilation effects as other nitrates.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Isosorbide mononitrate undergoes first-pass metabolism; it is sublingual nitroglycerin that avoids it.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Nitrates dilate rather than constrict vessels.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Isosorbide mononitrate is a nitrate and produces the same vasodilation effects via nitric oxide, just more gradually.

questions.stem: A nurse counsels a 57-year-old woman starting nitroglycerin that headache is a very common adverse effect. Approximately what proportion of patients who receive nitroglycerin report headache?

explanation.summary: More than 60% of patients receiving nitroglycerin report headache.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that more than 60% of patients who receive nitroglycerin report headache, making it the most common adverse effect of nitrates. The rate is significantly lower with long-acting isosorbide mononitrate.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Headache is far more common than 5% with nitroglycerin.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A 10% rate substantially understates the frequency the brick gives.
whyWrongByChoice.C: One quarter of patients understates the frequency the brick gives.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The brick's figure is higher than 40%; it exceeds 60%.

questions.stem: A 74-year-old man takes a sublingual nitroglycerin tablet for chest pain while seated. A few minutes later he stands up quickly, becomes dizzy, and briefly loses consciousness. Which of the following best explains this event?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Extensive first-pass metabolism of the dose

explanation.summary: Nitrate-induced vasodilation can cause postural (orthostatic) hypotension, producing dizziness and fainting.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick notes that because of the vasodilation nitroglycerin causes, the drug can produce postural, or orthostatic, hypotension that may result in dizziness and fainting. Standing quickly after a sublingual dose unmasks this drop in blood pressure.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Sublingual nitroglycerin avoids first-pass metabolism, and metabolism would reduce rather than produce hypotension.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Nitrates decrease, not increase, contraction force, and increased contractility would not cause fainting.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Tolerance is a loss of drug effect with continuous exposure; this patient shows an exaggerated effect after a single dose.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Nitrates dilate coronary arteries; they do not cause reflex coronary vasoconstriction.

questions.stem: A pharmacology student notes that a patient's response to nitroglycerin has become markedly attenuated after frequently repeated high doses. Which of the following terms describes this phenomenon?

explanation.summary: Nitrate tolerance is also called tachyphylaxis.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick defines nitrate tolerance, i.e., tachyphylaxis, as the marked attenuation in the magnitude of most of the pharmacological effects of nitrates that follows frequently repeated or continuous exposure to high doses.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Anaphylaxis is a severe allergic reaction, not a loss of drug effect.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Idiosyncrasy refers to an unusual individual response, not attenuation with repeated dosing.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Potentiation describes an enhanced effect, the opposite of what is observed.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Sensitization implies an increasing response over time, the opposite of tolerance.

questions.stem: A 69-year-old woman is prescribed a nitroglycerin transdermal patch. Which of the following instructions best reflects the recommended way to use the patch so as to reduce nitrate tolerance?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Wear the patch 24 hours a day and replace it at the same site each morning

choices.label: B
choices.text: Wear the patch for 12-14 hours, apply a second patch for the next 10-12 hours

choices.label: C
choices.text: Wear the patch for 12-14 hours, remove it for 10-12 hours, and rotate sites

choices.label: D
choices.text: Wear the patch for 4 hours only during chest pain and discard it afterward

choices.label: E
choices.text: Wear the patch for 6 hours, remove it for 18 hours, and reuse the same site

explanation.summary: The patch is worn for 12-14 hours, removed for 10-12 hours, and patch sites are rotated.
explanation.whyCorrect: Among the brick's suggestions for reducing nitrate tolerance, the patch should be worn on for 12-14 hours and off for 10-12 hours, and patch sites should be rotated. The off period provides the 10-12 hour nitrate-free interval that allows efficacy to return.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Continuous 24-hour wear provides no nitrate-free interval and promotes tolerance.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Applying a second patch during the off period eliminates the nitrate-free interval.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The patch is a delayed-onset, continuous-effect formulation, not a 4-hour as-needed treatment.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A 6-hour-on schedule does not match the 12-14 hour wear time the brick recommends.

questions.stem: A physician prescribes nitroglycerin ointment for a 61-year-old man. Which of the following dosing schedules is recommended to limit the development of tolerance?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Applied every 6 hours around the clock with no off period

choices.label: B
choices.text: Applied once daily and left in place continuously for 24 hours

choices.label: C
choices.text: Applied three times daily, 8 hours apart, with no off period

choices.label: D
choices.text: Applied twice daily, 12 hours apart, with no off period

choices.label: E
choices.text: Applied twice daily, 6 hours apart, then a 10-12 hour off period

explanation.summary: Nitroglycerin ointment is dosed twice daily, 6 hours apart, followed by a 10-12 hour off period.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick's suggestions for reducing nitrate tolerance state that the ointment is dosed twice daily, 6 hours apart, with a 10-12 hour off period. The off period supplies the nitrate-free interval that decreases the likelihood of tolerance.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Around-the-clock dosing provides continuous exposure with no nitrate-free interval.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A 24-hour continuous application offers no off period and encourages tolerance.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Three doses spaced 8 hours apart cover the full day with no nitrate-free interval.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Two doses 12 hours apart without an off period leave no 10-12 hour nitrate-free window.

questions.stem: A 65-year-old man admitted for unstable angina took his morning isosorbide mononitrate, received three doses of sublingual nitroglycerin in the emergency department, and has worn a transdermal nitroglycerin patch continuously since. Fourteen hours after presentation his chest pain has returned and is attributed to nitrate tolerance. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step regarding his nitrate therapy?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Apply a second transdermal patch to the other side of the chest

choices.label: B
choices.text: Begin a continuous intravenous nitroglycerin infusion

choices.label: C
choices.text: Double the dose of isosorbide mononitrate

choices.label: D
choices.text: Give an additional dose of sublingual nitroglycerin

choices.label: E
choices.text: Remove the patch to provide a 10-12 hour nitrate-free period

explanation.summary: Nitrate tolerance is managed by providing a 10-12 hour nitrate-free period, after which the nitrates become effective again.
explanation.whyCorrect: In the brick's case, JD has been receiving continuous nitrates for over 14 hours and the return of his chest pain indicates nitrate tolerance. To regain efficacy he needs a 'nitrate free' period of 10-12 hours, at which point the nitrates would be effective again.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A second patch increases continuous exposure rather than providing the needed nitrate-free interval.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A continuous IV infusion perpetuates uninterrupted nitrate exposure and will not restore efficacy.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Increasing the dosage does not necessarily prevent tolerance and can lead to more severe side effects.
whyWrongByChoice.D: More sublingual nitroglycerin adds nitrate exposure when the problem is tolerance from continuous exposure.

questions.stem: A 65-year-old man with unstable angina develops nitrate tolerance and continues to have chest pain. While a nitrate-free interval is provided, the team considers other approaches to relieve his ischemic pain. Which of the following procedural options is mentioned as a possible therapy?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Electrical cardioversion in the emergency department

choices.label: B
