Influx of calcium initiates processes such as muscle contraction, insulin secretion, and gene transcription. The pancreas is the endocrine site where L-type calcium influx triggers insulin release.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The adrenal cortex is not among the organs listed as sites of clinically relevant L-type channel expression.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Cortisol release is not the hormone secretion tied to L-type calcium channel influx.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Renin release from the kidney is not the process attributed to L-type calcium influx.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Thyroid hormone release is not the calcium-initiated process described for L-type channels.

questions.stem: A diagram of excitation-contraction coupling in muscle shows a motor nerve action potential, sodium entry across the sarcolemma, and calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum. In this scheme, the L-type calcium channel occupies a specific location and is functionally coupled to a release channel on the sarcoplasmic reticulum. Which of the following correctly pairs the location of the L-type channel with its coupled partner?

explanation.summary: In excitation-contraction coupling, the L-type calcium channel sits in the T-tubule and couples to the ryanodine receptor on the SR.
explanation.whyCorrect: In the excitation-contraction coupling diagram, the motor nerve action potential leads to sodium entry across the sarcolemma, and the L-type calcium channel is positioned in the T-tubule membrane. It is functionally linked to the ryanodine receptor (RYR) on the sarcoplasmic reticulum, which releases stored calcium into the cytosol to drive contraction.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The L-type channel is not a mitochondrial protein and is not coupled to a calcium ATPase in this scheme.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The motor nerve terminal releases neurotransmitter; the L-type channel in the diagram is on the muscle T-tubule.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The nuclear membrane and calmodulin are not the location and partner shown for the L-type channel.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The L-type channel is on the T-tubule, not the SR membrane, and its partner is the ryanodine receptor rather than an exchanger.

questions.stem: Calcium channel blockers are separated into two broad groups. A pharmacology exam asks which characteristic forms the basis of this classification. Which of the following is the correct basis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Degree of selectivity for cardiac tissue

choices.label: B
choices.text: Duration of antihypertensive action in hours

choices.label: E
choices.text: Route of elimination from the body (renal or hepatic)

explanation.summary: CCBs are classified by chemical structure according to whether a dihydropyridine ring is present.
explanation.whyCorrect: CCBs are classified based on their chemical structure, particularly the presence of a dihydropyridine. Broadly they are dihydropyridines (DHPs) or non-dihydropyridines (non-DHPs). DHP names end with the suffix '-dipine', and the two non-DHPs are verapamil and diltiazem.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cardiac versus vascular selectivity is a consequence of the classes, not the criterion used to define them.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Duration of action differs among CCBs but is not the basis of the DHP/non-DHP classification.
whyWrongByChoice.C: CYP3A4 inhibition potency differs between classes but does not define them.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Elimination route is not the classification criterion; the split is structural.

questions.stem: A resident sees an unfamiliar antihypertensive on a patient's medication list. The drug name ends in '-dipine'. Based on this naming convention, which of the following pharmacologic profiles should the resident predict for this drug?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Balanced venous and arterial dilation with reflex bradycardia

choices.label: B
choices.text: Potent arterial vasodilation with minimal SA nodal suppression

choices.label: C
choices.text: Potent CYP3A4 inhibition with marked constipation

choices.label: D
choices.text: Strong negative inotropy with strong AV nodal suppression

choices.label: E
choices.text: Strong SA nodal suppression with weak arterial vasodilation

explanation.summary: The '-dipine' suffix identifies a dihydropyridine, a potent arterial vasodilator with little nodal effect.
explanation.whyCorrect: The names of DHPs end with the suffix '-dipine' (for example amlodipine). Compared with the non-DHPs, DHPs are potent arterial vasodilators and have minimal effect on contractility and SA nodal activity, which is why they are preferred as antihypertensives.

whyWrongByChoice.A: CCBs relax arteriolar smooth muscle more than venous, and DHPs cause reflex tachycardia rather than bradycardia.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Potent CYP3A4 inhibition and constipation are associated with the non-DHP verapamil.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Strong negative inotropy and nodal suppression are non-DHP properties, not DHP properties.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Strong SA nodal suppression with weaker vasodilation describes the non-DHPs verapamil and diltiazem.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old woman with hypertension is started on felodipine. Her blood pressure falls over the following weeks. Which of the following hemodynamic changes best accounts for the antihypertensive effect of this drug?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Decreased cardiac output from slowing of SA nodal firing

choices.label: B
choices.text: Decreased plasma volume from renal sodium and water loss

choices.label: C
choices.text: Decreased renin release from juxtaglomerular cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: Decreased vascular resistance from arteriolar relaxation

choices.label: E
choices.text: Decreased venous return from venous smooth muscle relaxation

explanation.summary: CCBs lower blood pressure by relaxing arteriolar smooth muscle and reducing vascular resistance.
explanation.whyCorrect: CCBs inhibit calcium influx in vascular smooth muscle, decreasing the contractile process so the vessels relax. Arteriolar vascular smooth muscle is relaxed more than venous muscle. This relaxation reduces vascular resistance and lowers the pressure exerted by blood on the vascular wall, which is why CCBs are used to treat hypertension.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Felodipine is a DHP with minimal SA nodal effect; its antihypertensive action is vascular.
whyWrongByChoice.B: CCBs do not lower blood pressure by promoting natriuresis or reducing plasma volume.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Reduced renin release is not the mechanism by which CCBs lower blood pressure.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Venous smooth muscle is relaxed less than arteriolar muscle, so venodilation is not the primary mechanism.

questions.stem: A 67-year-old man with hypertension and angina is treated with diltiazem, which decreases both his heart rate and cardiac contractility. The heart's dependence on a particular calcium-handling process for each action potential explains why L-type channel inhibition has these effects. Which of the following is that process?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Calcium-calmodulin activation of myosin light-chain kinase

choices.label: B
choices.text: Calcium-independent release of stored calcium by inositol trisphosphate

choices.label: C
choices.text: Calcium-induced calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum

choices.label: D
choices.text: Phosphorylation of myosin light chain by a calcium-dependent kinase

choices.label: E
choices.text: Sodium-driven calcium extrusion by the sodium-calcium exchanger

explanation.summary: Cardiac muscle relies on calcium-induced calcium release, so blocking L-type influx slows rate and reduces contractility.
explanation.whyCorrect: Cardiac muscle depends on calcium-induced calcium release (CICR) for initiating each action potential and for the sustained contractility of the cardiac muscle. Inhibition of L-type calcium channels in the heart therefore slows the heart rate and reduces the force of contractility, and it decreases the rate of SA and AV nodal firing.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Calcium-calmodulin activation of myosin light-chain kinase is the smooth muscle contractile pathway, not the cardiac trigger.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Cardiac muscle is described as depending on calcium-induced calcium release, not a calcium-independent IP3 mechanism.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Myosin light-chain phosphorylation drives smooth muscle contraction; cardiac contraction depends on CICR and troponin C.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Calcium extrusion by an exchanger is not the process the heart relies on to initiate each contraction.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman presents with a narrow-complex tachycardia diagnosed as atrioventricular nodal reentrant tachycardia. Intravenous diltiazem terminates the rhythm. Which of the following best describes the tissue targeted by this drug to achieve its antiarrhythmic effect?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Accessory pathway tissue bypassing the AV node

choices.label: B
choices.text: Atrial myocardium surrounding the pulmonary veins

choices.label: C
choices.text: Fast-response tissue of the His-Purkinje system

choices.label: D
choices.text: Fast-response tissue of the ventricular myocardium

choices.label: E
choices.text: Slow-response tissue of the SA and AV nodes

explanation.summary: Non-DHPs are antiarrhythmic because they target the slow-response tissues of the SA and AV nodes.
explanation.whyCorrect: Calcium channel blockers such as verapamil and diltiazem exhibit antiarrhythmic properties by primarily targeting the slow response tissues in the SA and AV nodes. They are effective in managing supraventricular tachycardias that depend on AV node conduction, such as atrioventricular nodal reentrant tachycardia and atrioventricular reentrant tachycardia.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Non-DHPs work on the AV node itself, on which the reentrant circuit depends, rather than on accessory pathway tissue.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Atrial myocardium near the pulmonary veins is not the tissue targeted by non-DHPs for antiarrhythmic effect.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The His-Purkinje system is fast-response tissue; non-DHPs act on the slow-response nodal tissue.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Ventricular myocardium is fast-response tissue and is not the primary antiarrhythmic target of non-DHPs.

questions.stem: A 42-year-old man has a persistent sinus tachycardia of 120/min that has not responded to conservative measures, and a non-dihydropyridine CCB is prescribed. Which of the following electrophysiologic changes is expected to correct his rhythm?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Accelerated conduction through the His-Purkinje system

choices.label: B
choices.text: Decreased rate of SA nodal firing

choices.label: C
choices.text: Increased automaticity of the AV junction

explanation.summary: Non-DHPs are negative chronotropes that decrease SA nodal firing, correcting fast rhythms such as sinus tachycardia.
explanation.whyCorrect: The inhibition of calcium influx by CCBs decreases the rate of SA and AV nodal firing. These agents have negative chronotropic effects, and this property can correct abnormal rhythms such as fast heart rates (sinus tachycardia). Non-DHPs are potent at suppressing SA nodal activity and are used for their negative chronotropic activity.

whyWrongByChoice.A: CCBs slow nodal firing; they do not accelerate His-Purkinje conduction.
whyWrongByChoice.C: CCBs suppress rather than increase nodal automaticity.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Ventricular refractoriness is not the mechanism by which CCBs slow a sinus tachycardia.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Prolonging the atrial action potential is not the described effect of CCBs on the heart.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old woman with atrial fibrillation requires a calcium channel blocker for ventricular rate control. Her echocardiogram shows mildly reduced left ventricular contractility, so the physician wants the agent that provides strong SA/AV nodal suppression while depressing contractility the least. Using the comparative effects of the CCBs, which drug is the best choice?

explanation.summary: Diltiazem matches verapamil's nodal suppression (5) but suppresses contractility much less (2 vs 4).
explanation.whyCorrect: In the comparison of CCB effects (5 highest to 1 lowest ability to inhibit activity), verapamil scores 4 for contractility and 5 for SA nodal activity, whereas diltiazem scores 2 for contractility and 5 for SA nodal activity. Diltiazem therefore delivers the same nodal (chronotropic) suppression as verapamil with substantially less negative inotropy, making it the better non-DHP when contractility is a concern.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Amlodipine has minimal contractility effect (1) but also minimal SA nodal suppression (1), so it would not control the rate.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Felodipine is a DHP with negligible nodal suppression and is not a rate-control agent.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Nifedipine is a DHP that acts as a vasodilator and does not provide nodal rate control.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Verapamil provides the needed nodal suppression (5) but has the strongest contractility suppression (4) of the CCBs compared.

questions.stem: A 61-year-old man with hypertension is switched from immediate-release nifedipine to verapamil. His blood pressure falls, yet his resting heart rate decreases from 78 to 62/min rather than rising as it did on nifedipine. Which property of verapamil best explains the absence of a reflex rise in heart rate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Blockade of the sympathetic reflex arc

choices.label: B
choices.text: Direct suppression of SA nodal firing

explanation.summary: Non-DHPs do not cause reflex tachycardia because they directly suppress the SA node.
explanation.whyCorrect: Reflex tachycardia occurs with immediate-release nifedipine because its rapid blood pressure drop triggers sympathetic activation. Verapamil and diltiazem are non-DHPs that are less likely to produce this response because they have potent SA nodal suppression; verapamil scores highest (5) in suppressing SA nodal activity. The direct negative chronotropic action overrides any reflex increase in rate, so the heart rate falls.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Verapamil does not block the sympathetic reflex; it directly slows the SA node.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Half-life differences explain the pharmacokinetic contrast between nifedipine and amlodipine, not verapamil's bradycardic effect.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Slow absorption explains amlodipine's reduced reflex tachycardia, not the heart rate fall seen with verapamil.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Verapamil still produces substantial arterial vasodilation (score 4); the lack of tachycardia is due to nodal suppression, not weak vasodilation.

questions.stem: A 76-year-old woman with third-degree AV block and a permanent pacemaker has hypertension that requires a calcium channel blocker. Which of the following agents is the most appropriate choice for her?

explanation.summary: DHPs such as amlodipine are the CCBs of choice when non-DHPs are contraindicated by high-grade heart block.
explanation.whyCorrect: Non-DHPs are contraindicated in patients with 2nd and 3rd degree heart blocks because they further suppress SA/AV nodal activity. DHPs such as amlodipine have minimal SA nodal suppression (score 1) and act as potent arterial vasodilators, so amlodipine lowers blood pressure without worsening conduction.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Diltiazem is a non-DHP that also suppresses SA/AV nodal activity and is contraindicated here.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Dose reduction does not remove the contraindication; non-DHPs should be avoided in high-grade block.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Verapamil is a non-DHP and is contraindicated in 2nd and 3rd degree heart block.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Combining two non-DHPs compounds nodal suppression and is contraindicated in heart block.

questions.stem: A pharmacist is comparing the pharmacokinetics of two dihydropyridines. Immediate-release nifedipine has a plasma half-life of about 1.8 hours. Which of the following is the approximate plasma half-life of amlodipine?

explanation.summary: Amlodipine has a long plasma half-life of 35 to 50 hours.
explanation.whyCorrect: CCBs show significant differences in their pharmacokinetics. Immediate-release nifedipine is rapidly absorbed with a half-life of about 1.8 hours. In contrast, amlodipine is absorbed slowly and has a prolonged effect, with a plasma half-life of 35 to 50 hours.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A half-life of a few hours is closer to immediate-release nifedipine, not amlodipine.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Six to eight hours is far shorter than amlodipine's 35 to 50 hour half-life.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Seven to ten days is the time for amlodipine to reach steady state with daily dosing, not its half-life.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Twelve to eighteen hours underestimates amlodipine's half-life.

questions.stem: A 49-year-old man with newly diagnosed hypertension began amlodipine 5 mg daily three days ago. He returns because his home blood pressure readings are only slightly lower than before. He is taking the drug as prescribed and has no adverse effects. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Add verapamil to enhance vasodilation at this visit

choices.label: B
choices.text: Continue the current dose and reassess after steady state

choices.label: C
choices.text: Discontinue amlodipine today as an early treatment failure

choices.label: D
choices.text: Double the amlodipine dose to 10 mg daily at this visit

choices.label: E
choices.text: Switch to immediate-release nifedipine for a faster effect

explanation.summary: Amlodipine's plasma level and effect build gradually over 7 to 10 days, so early readings underestimate its full effect.
explanation.whyCorrect: Amlodipine is absorbed slowly and has a prolonged effect. With a plasma half-life of 35 to 50 hours, its plasma levels and effects gradually increase over 7 to 10 days of daily administration at a constant dose, resulting in a steady-state concentration. At three days the drug has not reached steady state, so the appropriate step is to continue the same dose and reassess once the full effect is established.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Adding a non-DHP is not indicated; the current drug simply has not reached its full effect.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Three days is too early to judge failure of a drug that takes 7 to 10 days to reach steady state.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Increasing the dose before steady state is reached risks overshooting once levels finish accumulating over 7 to 10 days.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Immediate-release nifedipine causes a sudden blood pressure drop with reflex tachycardia and is not a better choice.

questions.stem: A 64-year-old man taking simvastatin for hyperlipidemia is started on verapamil for supraventricular tachycardia. Two months later he develops diffuse muscle pain and an elevated creatine kinase. Which of the following best explains this drug interaction?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Simvastatin induced CYP3A4 and raised verapamil levels

choices.label: B
choices.text: Simvastatin inhibited renal excretion of verapamil

choices.label: C
choices.text: Verapamil and simvastatin competed for the same L-type channel

choices.label: D
choices.text: Verapamil displaced simvastatin from plasma proteins

choices.label: E
choices.text: Verapamil inhibited CYP3A4 and raised simvastatin levels

explanation.summary: Verapamil is a potent CYP3A4 inhibitor and raises levels of CYP3A4 substrates such as simvastatin and atorvastatin.
explanation.whyCorrect: All CCBs are substrates of CYP3A4, and the non-DHPs are potent CYP3A4 inhibitors. Verapamil in particular is a strong CYP3A4 substrate and can cause clinically relevant drug interactions with other CYP3A4 substrates such as simvastatin and atorvastatin. Inhibition of the statin's metabolism raises its exposure, which can produce muscle toxicity.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Simvastatin is a CYP3A4 substrate, not an inducer; the perpetrator in this interaction is verapamil.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The interaction described involves hepatic CYP3A4 metabolism, not renal excretion.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Statins do not act on L-type calcium channels; the interaction is pharmacokinetic.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The interaction is metabolic through CYP3A4, not protein-binding displacement.

questions.stem: A clinical pharmacist notes that oral CCBs reach the systemic circulation in much smaller amounts than the dose administered, and that coadministered CYP3A4 inhibitors markedly increase their bioavailability. Which of the following properties shared by all CCBs best accounts for these observations?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Active secretion into the renal tubule

choices.label: E
choices.text: Rapid biliary excretion of unchanged drug

explanation.summary: All CCBs undergo extensive first-pass metabolism as CYP3A4 substrates, so CYP3A4 inhibitors raise their bioavailability.
explanation.whyCorrect: CCBs go through extensive first-pass metabolism, and all CCBs are substrates of CYP3A4. Because of this, the bioavailability of CCBs may be increased by strong CYP3A4 inhibitors such as macrolides (azithromycin, clarithromycin), antiretroviral agents, and grapefruit juice. These drug-drug interactions are clinically relevant and should be monitored.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Renal tubular secretion does not explain a bioavailability change produced by CYP3A4 inhibitors.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Erythrocyte binding is not a described property of CCBs and would not be affected by CYP3A4 inhibition.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Poor dissolution would not be corrected by CYP3A4 inhibitors; the limiting step is hepatic first-pass metabolism.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Biliary excretion of unchanged drug is not the mechanism; CCBs are metabolized extensively by CYP3A4.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old woman started amlodipine for hypertension four days ago. She now reports a throbbing headache, facial flushing, and an awareness of her heartbeat. She has no chest pain, and her examination is otherwise normal. Which of the following is the most likely explanation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Allergic drug reaction requiring immediate withdrawal

choices.label: B
choices.text: Excessive SA nodal suppression by the drug

choices.label: C
choices.text: Expected vasodilatory effects after starting the drug

choices.label: D
choices.text: Fluid retention from increased renal sodium reabsorption

choices.label: E
choices.text: Hypertensive urgency from an inadequate starting dose

explanation.summary: Headache, flushing, and palpitations are common CCB adverse reactions, particularly right after the drug is started.
explanation.whyCorrect: Headache, flushing, and palpitations are associated with CCB use, particularly after the drug is initiated. They reflect the vasodilation produced by the drug and are listed among the expected adverse reactions rather than a sign of treatment failure or allergy.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Headache, flushing, and palpitations are pharmacologic adverse reactions, not features of an allergic reaction.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Amlodipine is a DHP with minimal SA nodal suppression; palpitations here are not from nodal suppression.
whyWrongByChoice.D: CCB adverse effects are not caused by renal fluid retention; even CCB edema is due to hydrostatic pressure.
whyWrongByChoice.E: These symptoms are recognized adverse effects of the drug itself, not evidence of uncontrolled hypertension.

questions.stem: A 59-year-old man on amlodipine develops bilateral pedal edema. A diagram of the mechanism shows that the drug dilates one segment of the microcirculation but not another, and this mismatch raises capillary pressure and permeability, forcing fluid into surrounding tissue. Which of the following vessels is NOT dilated by the drug, creating this mismatch?

explanation.summary: CCB pedal edema arises because arterioles are dilated while venules are not.
explanation.whyCorrect: Amlodipine dilates only arterioles and not the venules. Dilation of the arterial side with undilated venous capillaries increases capillary pressure and capillary permeability, leading to expulsion of fluid into the surrounding tissue and pedal edema. The edema is therefore not due to fluid retention.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Arterioles are the vessels that are dilated by the drug; their dilation is what raises capillary pressure.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Capillaries are where pressure and permeability rise; the mismatch is between arterioles and venules.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The mechanism concerns the precapillary arteriole versus the postcapillary venule, not large conduit arteries.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Lymphatic vessels are not part of the described mechanism of CCB-induced edema.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old man with a family history of hypertension has an average blood pressure of 155/95 mm Hg and a heart rate of 80/min. He is prescribed amlodipine and asks what symptoms he should watch for. Which of the following symptoms should he be told could signal a decrease in his heart rate?

explanation.summary: Patients starting a CCB should report lethargy, which could be a sign of a decreased heart rate.
explanation.whyCorrect: When amlodipine is started for hypertension, the patient is told that it is a commonly prescribed and generally safe medication but should watch for palpitations and dizziness. He should also check for any feeling of lethargy, which could be a sign of a decrease in heart rate, and should avoid grapefruit juice because it interferes with the drug's CYP3A4 metabolism.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Ankle swelling reflects CCB-induced peripheral edema from arteriolar dilation, not bradycardia.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Constipation is an adverse effect associated with verapamil and does not indicate a slowed heart rate.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Flushing is a vasodilatory adverse effect, not a sign of a slowed heart rate.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Headache is a vasodilatory adverse effect seen after initiation, not a marker of decreased heart rate.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old man has exertional chest pain from stable angina. His physician wants a calcium channel blocker whose primary benefit comes from reducing cardiac contractility and heart rate to lower myocardial oxygen demand, rather than from vasodilation alone. Which of the following is the most appropriate choice?

explanation.summary: Non-DHPs such as verapamil reduce contractility and heart rate, lowering oxygen demand in angina.
explanation.whyCorrect: In angina, increased demand for cardiac contraction causes chest pain that can result in ischemia. The negative inotropic effect of CCBs decreases the contractility of the heart and lowers O2 demand, so they are used as antianginal agents. Non-DHPs are potent at suppressing contractility (verapamil scores 4) and SA nodal activity (5), and they decrease cardiac contractility and heart rate to treat angina and arrhythmias.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Amlodipine is a DHP with minimal effect on contractility (score 1) and heart rate; its benefit is vasodilation.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Felodipine is a DHP with negligible negative inotropic or chronotropic effect.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Nicardipine is a DHP that lowers pressure by arterial vasodilation, not by reducing contractility.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Nifedipine is a DHP vasodilator whose rapid action can cause reflex tachycardia, increasing rather than reducing rate.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man taking verapamil for atrial fibrillation develops symptomatic bradycardia. The team discusses agents whose effect on SA nodal firing is opposite to that of verapamil. Which of the following drugs increases the rate of SA nodal firing and is therefore a positive chronotropic agent?

explanation.summary: Epinephrine increases SA nodal firing (positive chronotropy), the opposite of verapamil's effect.
explanation.whyCorrect: Verapamil is a non-DHP with potent SA nodal suppression and acts as a potent negative chronotropic agent. Epinephrine increases the rate of SA nodal firing and hence is a positive chronotropic agent, making its chronotropic effect opposite to verapamil's.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Amlodipine is a DHP with minimal direct nodal effect; it does not increase SA nodal firing directly.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Diltiazem is a non-DHP that, like verapamil, suppresses SA nodal firing (score 5).
whyWrongByChoice.D: Felodipine is a DHP with negligible direct effect on SA nodal firing.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Nifedipine is a DHP; any rate increase with it is reflex sympathetic activation, not direct positive chronotropy.

questions.stem: A student is asked to list the organs that express L-type calcium channels. In addition to the heart and vascular smooth muscle, which of the following tissues is a site of L-type calcium channel expression?

explanation.summary: L-type calcium channels are found in the heart, skeletal muscle, smooth muscle, and pancreas.
explanation.whyCorrect: L-type calcium channels are found in many organs, such as the heart, skeletal muscle, smooth muscle, and pancreas. The organs with the most clinically relevant effect for CCBs are cardiac and smooth muscle, but skeletal muscle is also a site of L-type channel expression, as shown in the excitation-contraction coupling diagram with the L-type channel in the T-tubule.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Adipose tissue is not identified as an L-type calcium channel site.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Erythrocytes are not a described site of L-type calcium channel expression.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hepatocytes are not listed among the organs expressing L-type calcium channels.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Renal tubular epithelium is not among the tissues named for L-type channel expression.

questions.stem: A pharmacology table rates three calcium channel blockers on a 1-to-5 scale (5 = greatest inhibition) for arterial vasodilation, contractility, and SA nodal automaticity. One drug is rated 4 for arterial vasodilation, 4 for contractility, and 5 for SA nodal activity. Which of the following drugs has this profile?

explanation.summary: Verapamil is rated 4 (vasodilation), 4 (contractility), and 5 (SA nodal) in the CCB comparison table.
explanation.whyCorrect: In the comparison of CCB effects, amlodipine (the DHP prototype) scores 5 for arterial vasodilation, 1 for contractility, and 1 for SA nodal activity; verapamil scores 4, 4, and 5; and diltiazem scores 3, 2, and 5. The profile of strong vasodilation, strong negative inotropy, and maximal SA nodal suppression is verapamil, which is why it is often used as an antiarrhythmic.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Amlodipine is rated 5 for vasodilation but only 1 for contractility and 1 for SA nodal activity.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Diltiazem is rated 3 for vasodilation, 2 for contractility, and 5 for SA nodal activity.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Felodipine is a DHP and does not have strong negative inotropic or SA nodal effects.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Nifedipine is a DHP; DHPs share amlodipine's profile of potent vasodilation with minimal nodal or inotropic effect.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man with newly diagnosed stage 1 hypertension is started on lisinopril. The drug lowers his blood pressure by interfering with a specific step in the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system. Which of the following steps does lisinopril inhibit?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Binding of angiotensin II to its type 1 receptor

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cleavage of angiotensinogen into angiotensin I

choices.label: C
choices.text: Conversion of angiotensin I into angiotensin II

choices.label: D
choices.text: Release of aldosterone directly from the adrenal cortex

choices.label: E
choices.text: Release of renin from juxtaglomerular cells

explanation.summary: ACE inhibitors block angiotensin-converting enzyme, halting formation of angiotensin II.
explanation.whyCorrect: ACE, found largely in the lungs, catalyzes conversion of angiotensin I to angiotensin II. By blocking this enzyme, ACE inhibitors reduce angiotensin II, decreasing vasoconstriction and aldosterone release and thereby lowering blood pressure.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Blocking the angiotensin II type 1 receptor is the mechanism of ARBs (sartans), not ACE inhibitors.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Renin, not ACE, cleaves angiotensinogen into angiotensin I; ACE inhibitors do not affect this step.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Aldosterone secretion falls indirectly because angiotensin II is reduced, not through direct blockade at the adrenal cortex.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Inhibiting renin release is the mechanism of renin inhibitors such as aliskiren.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old woman who developed a persistent dry cough on enalapril is switched to losartan, which controls her blood pressure without the cough. By what mechanism does losartan lower blood pressure?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Blocking aldosterone receptors in the collecting duct

choices.label: C
choices.text: Directly relaxing arteriolar smooth muscle independent of angiotensin

choices.label: E
choices.text: Inhibiting renin release from the kidney

explanation.summary: ARBs block the angiotensin II type 1 receptor, preventing angiotensin II from acting.
explanation.whyCorrect: ARBs such as losartan block angiotensin II at its type 1 receptor. Angiotensin II is still produced (ACE is not inhibited) but cannot exert vasoconstriction or promote aldosterone release. Because bradykinin metabolism is unaffected, ARBs have a much lower incidence of cough than ACE inhibitors.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Blocking aldosterone receptors describes spironolactone, not an ARB.
whyWrongByChoice.C: ARBs work through the angiotensin receptor, not by direct nonspecific arteriolar relaxation like a calcium channel blocker.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Inhibiting ACE is the mechanism of the -pril drugs; losartan is an ARB and does not block ACE.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Renin inhibitors act one step earlier by blocking renin; ARBs act at the receptor.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old woman started on lisinopril three weeks ago presents with a dry, hacking cough that is worse at night. She has no fever, wheezing, or sputum production. Accumulation of which of the following substances most likely explains her cough?

explanation.summary: ACE inhibitor cough is caused by accumulation of bradykinin.
explanation.whyCorrect: ACE normally degrades bradykinin. When ACE is inhibited, bradykinin accumulates; as a bronchoconstrictive inflammatory mediator it increases vascular permeability and causes bronchial smooth muscle contraction, producing a dry cough. Switching to an ARB, which does not affect bradykinin, usually relieves it.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Aldosterone is reduced by RAAS inhibition and is unrelated to the cough.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Angiotensin II levels fall with an ACE inhibitor and do not cause the cough.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Histamine mediates allergic reactions but is not the ACE inhibitor cough mechanism described in the brick.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Potassium retention causes hyperkalemia, not cough.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man with heart failure taking lisinopril and spironolactone is found on routine labs to have a serum potassium of 5.9 mEq/L. Which mechanism best explains the hyperkalemia attributable to his ACE inhibitor?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Bradykinin-induced shift of potassium out of cells

choices.label: C
choices.text: Direct blockade of renal potassium channels

choices.label: E
choices.text: Increased glomerular filtration promoting potassium loss

explanation.summary: RAAS inhibition lowers aldosterone, reducing renal potassium excretion.
explanation.whyCorrect: By reducing angiotensin II, ACE inhibitors reduce aldosterone secretion from the adrenal cortex. Less aldosterone means less renal tubular secretion of potassium, leading to potassium retention and hyperkalemia. Risk is amplified by potassium-sparing agents such as spironolactone.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Bradykinin causes cough and angioedema, not a transcellular potassium shift here.
whyWrongByChoice.C: ACE inhibitors act through aldosterone, not by directly blocking renal potassium channels.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Aldosterone is decreased, not increased, by an ACE inhibitor.
whyWrongByChoice.E: ACE inhibitors tend to lower GFR, and this is not the mechanism of hyperkalemia.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old woman with dehydration from several days of gastroenteritis is started on ramipril for hypertension. Two days later her serum creatinine rises and her glomerular filtration rate falls. Which renal hemodynamic change best explains this acute decline in GFR?

choices.label: E
choices.text: Physical obstruction of the renal tubule

explanation.summary: ACE inhibitors dilate the efferent arteriole, lowering GFR, especially in volume-depleted patients.
explanation.whyCorrect: Under normal conditions angiotensin II constricts the efferent arteriole to maintain glomerular pressure and GFR. ACE inhibitors and ARBs block this, dilating the efferent arteriole and reducing glomerular hydrostatic pressure, which acutely lowers GFR. This prerenal effect is pronounced with dehydration or heart failure.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Afferent constriction is not the mechanism; the brick attributes the GFR drop to loss of efferent tone.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Efferent constriction is the normal angiotensin II effect that the drug blocks, not causes.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Glomerular hydrostatic pressure decreases, not increases, which is why GFR falls.
whyWrongByChoice.E: This is a prerenal hemodynamic effect, not a postrenal tubular obstruction.

questions.stem: A 65-year-old man maintained on lisinopril begins taking ibuprofen several times daily for arthritis pain. He subsequently develops acute kidney injury. Why does combining an NSAID with an ACE inhibitor increase this risk?

choices.label: A
choices.text: NSAIDs block prostaglandin-mediated dilation of the afferent arteriole

choices.label: B
choices.text: NSAIDs dilate the efferent arteriole, compounding the ACE inhibitor's effect

choices.label: C
choices.text: NSAIDs directly block renal potassium excretion

choices.label: D
choices.text: NSAIDs increase renin secretion from the kidney

choices.label: E
choices.text: NSAIDs sharply increase circulating angiotensin II levels

explanation.summary: NSAIDs constrict the afferent arteriole while ACE inhibitors dilate the efferent, together dropping GFR.
explanation.whyCorrect: NSAIDs inhibit prostaglandins that normally dilate the afferent arteriole, reducing inflow. Coupled with efferent dilation from the ACE inhibitor, glomerular filtration pressure falls markedly, greatly increasing the risk of acute kidney injury. The brick lists this as a key drug interaction to avoid.

whyWrongByChoice.B: NSAIDs constrict the afferent arteriole by blocking prostaglandins; they do not dilate the efferent arteriole.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The shared risk here is reduced GFR and AKI, not a direct effect on potassium channels.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Increased renin is not the mechanism; reduced afferent dilation is.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The risk stems from altered renal blood flow, not a surge in angiotensin II.

questions.stem: A 54-year-old African American man develops swelling of the lips and tongue several hours after taking his first dose of an ACE inhibitor. Which of the following is the most feared complication of this reaction?

explanation.summary: Angioedema from ACE inhibitors is dangerous because it can obstruct the airway.
explanation.whyCorrect: Increased bradykinin can trigger angioedema, causing swelling of the face, lips, tongue, and upper airway. Airway obstruction is the most feared complication and can be fatal. African American patients have about a 4.5-fold greater risk of ACE inhibitor-induced angioedema.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Acute kidney injury is a hemodynamic effect unrelated to airway swelling.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hyperkalemia is a separate metabolic adverse effect, not the danger of angioedema swelling.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Dry cough is a common, non-life-threatening bradykinin effect, not the feared angioedema complication.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Rebound hypertension is not the described complication of angioedema.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old woman with chronic hypertension who is 10 weeks pregnant asks whether her blood pressure medication is safe to continue. Which of the following antihypertensive classes is contraindicated because it is teratogenic and can cause fetal kidney injury?

explanation.summary: ACE inhibitors and ARBs are contraindicated in pregnancy due to teratogenicity.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick lists pregnancy as a contraindication to ACE inhibitors and ARBs because they are teratogenic and can cause fetal kidney injury. These agents should be stopped in a patient who is or may become pregnant.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Alpha-methyldopa is not an ACE inhibitor and is not the class contraindicated for teratogenicity here.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Beta-blockers are not the class flagged in the brick as teratogenic RAAS inhibitors.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Calcium channel blockers are not identified as the pregnancy-contraindicated class here.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Thiazide diuretics are not the teratogenic class discussed in this brick.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old man with known bilateral renal artery stenosis is being evaluated for blood pressure management. Why are ACE inhibitors and ARBs contraindicated in this patient?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Reduced renal blood flow makes the kidneys dependent on efferent constriction

choices.label: B
choices.text: They cause an excessive rise in circulating angiotensin II and aldosterone

choices.label: C
choices.text: They cause hyperkalemia by a mechanism independent of renal potassium handling

choices.label: D
choices.text: They increase urinary protein loss and worsen the degree of stenosis

choices.label: E
choices.text: They provoke reflex tachycardia that worsens renal perfusion pressure

explanation.summary: In bilateral renal artery stenosis, kidneys rely on efferent constriction to maintain filtration.
explanation.whyCorrect: With bilateral renal artery stenosis, renal blood flow is already low, and the kidneys depend on angiotensin II-mediated efferent constriction to maintain glomerular pressure. ACE inhibitors and ARBs remove that tone, risking a decline in renal function, so they are contraindicated.

whyWrongByChoice.B: These drugs lower or block angiotensin II activity; they do not raise it excessively.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hyperkalemia is a separate concern; the contraindication in stenosis is about renal perfusion and filtration.
whyWrongByChoice.D: In stenosis the concern is falling GFR from loss of efferent tone, not increased proteinuria.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Reflex tachycardia is not the reason cited in the brick for this contraindication.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man with diabetic chronic kidney disease is found to have proteinuria on urinalysis. Which medication class is first-line to reduce his proteinuria and slow progression of his renal disease?

explanation.summary: ACE inhibitors and ARBs are first-line to reduce proteinuria in CKD.
explanation.whyCorrect: In chronic kidney disease with proteinuria, ACE inhibitors and ARBs are first-line. By dilating the efferent arteriole they lower glomerular hydrostatic pressure, decreasing microalbuminuria and slowing progression of renal disease.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Beta-blockers are used for cardiac indications and do not specifically reduce proteinuria.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Calcium channel blockers control blood pressure but are not first-line for proteinuria here.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Loop diuretics manage fluid balance but do not specifically reduce proteinuria.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Statins lower cholesterol and do not directly reduce proteinuria.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old man with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction is started on an ACE inhibitor in addition to a beta-blocker and a loop diuretic. Beyond lowering blood pressure, what long-term benefit do ACE inhibitors provide in heart failure?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Increasing heart rate to improve cardiac output

choices.label: D
choices.text: Promoting sodium and water retention to raise preload

choices.label: E
choices.text: Raising serum potassium to protect the myocardium

explanation.summary: In heart failure, ACE inhibitors prevent maladaptive cardiac fibrosis and remodeling.
explanation.whyCorrect: By reducing angiotensin II, ACE inhibitors prevent the ventricular fibrosis and abnormal cardiac remodeling that angiotensin II promotes. This is why they are first-line in heart failure alongside beta-blockers and loop diuretics.

whyWrongByChoice.A: ACE inhibitors reduce afterload; they do not increase it.
whyWrongByChoice.B: ACE inhibitors do not act by increasing heart rate.
whyWrongByChoice.D: They reduce sodium and water retention by lowering aldosterone, not promote it.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Raising potassium is an adverse effect, not a therapeutic benefit.

questions.stem: A physician considers adding an ARB to a patient already taking an ACE inhibitor in an effort to improve blood pressure control. Why is combining these two classes generally avoided?

choices.label: A
choices.text: ARBs neutralize the antihypertensive effect of ACE inhibitors

choices.label: B
choices.text: The combination causes severe reflex tachycardia

choices.label: C
choices.text: The combination increases the risk of hyperkalemia

choices.label: D
choices.text: The combination markedly increases the incidence of dry cough

choices.label: E
choices.text: They chemically inactivate one another in the bloodstream

explanation.summary: ACE inhibitors and ARBs should not be combined because risks rise with no added benefit.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that ACE inhibitors and ARBs should not be used together because of additive adverse effects, including hyperkalemia, acute kidney injury, and an increased risk of angioedema, while the combination has not been shown to provide additional clinical benefit.

whyWrongByChoice.A: ARBs do not neutralize ACE inhibitors; both lower blood pressure by acting on the same pathway.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Reflex tachycardia is not the reason the combination is avoided.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Increased cough is not the cited reason; the concern is hyperkalemia, AKI, and angioedema.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The drugs do not chemically inactivate each other; the concern is additive physiologic toxicity.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old man arrives in the emergency department after a motorcycle collision with significant blood loss. His blood pressure is 82/50 mm Hg. In response to the fall in blood pressure and blood volume, renin is secreted into the circulation. The cells that release renin are best described as which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Endothelial cells of the pulmonary capillaries

choices.label: B
choices.text: Modified smooth muscle cells of the afferent arteriole

choices.label: C
choices.text: Principal cells of the renal collecting duct

choices.label: D
choices.text: Specialized epithelial cells of the distal tubule

choices.label: E
choices.text: Steroid-secreting cells of the adrenal cortex

explanation.summary: Renin is released by juxtaglomerular cells, which are modified smooth muscle cells of the afferent arteriole.
explanation.whyCorrect: The first step of the RAAS pathway is secretion of the protease renin by the kidney's juxtaglomerular (JG) cells. The JG cells are modified smooth muscle cells of the renal afferent arteriole that sense low blood flow, blood volume, or blood pressure and respond by releasing renin.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The lungs are the primary site of angiotensin-converting enzyme, not of renin release.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Principal cells of the collecting duct are targets of aldosterone (sodium reabsorption and potassium secretion), not the source of renin.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The macula densa cells of the distal tubule sense sodium chloride delivery and signal for renin release, but they do not secrete renin themselves.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The adrenal cortex releases aldosterone in response to angiotensin II; it does not secrete renin.

questions.stem: Once released from the kidney, renin acts on an inactive circulating protein to generate angiotensin I. The organ that synthesizes this inactive precursor protein is which of the following?

explanation.summary: Angiotensinogen, the substrate for renin, is made by the liver.
explanation.whyCorrect: After renin is released it travels to the liver, which makes the inactive protein angiotensinogen. In the liver, renin cleaves angiotensinogen into angiotensin I, the precursor hormone to angiotensin II.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The adrenal gland releases aldosterone in response to angiotensin II.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The kidney releases renin, the enzyme, but does not make the angiotensinogen substrate.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The lung is where ACE converts angiotensin I to angiotensin II; it does not produce angiotensinogen.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The posterior pituitary releases ADH in response to angiotensin II; it does not make angiotensinogen.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old woman on captopril develops a dry cough attributed to bradykinin accumulation. The enzyme inhibited by captopril, which normally degrades bradykinin and converts angiotensin I to angiotensin II, is expressed primarily in which of the following organs?

explanation.summary: ACE is primarily expressed in the lungs.
explanation.whyCorrect: Angiotensin I travels to the lungs, where angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) converts it into the peptide hormone angiotensin II. The primary expression of ACE in the lungs, and the bradykinin accumulation that follows its inhibition, is what leads to the ACE inhibitor cough.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The adrenal cortex secretes aldosterone in response to angiotensin II.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The hypothalamus mediates thirst in response to angiotensin II; it is not the site of ACE expression.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The kidney's juxtaglomerular cells release renin; ACE is not primarily a renal enzyme.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The liver produces angiotensinogen and is where renin cleaves it to angiotensin I, but ACE is not primarily expressed there.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man who has been working outdoors in the heat without drinking fluids becomes hypovolemic and reports intense thirst. Activation of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system contributes to this symptom. Which of the following mediators acts on the hypothalamus to stimulate thirst?

explanation.summary: Angiotensin II acts on the hypothalamus to stimulate thirst and on the posterior pituitary to release ADH.
explanation.whyCorrect: Among the downstream targets of angiotensin II shown in the RAAS pathway are the hypothalamus, where it stimulates thirst, and the posterior pituitary, where it promotes ADH release. Together with vasoconstriction, efferent arteriolar constriction, and aldosterone release, these effects raise blood pressure and expand blood volume.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Aldosterone acts on renal principal and intercalated cells to reabsorb sodium and secrete potassium and hydrogen; it does not mediate thirst.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Angiotensin I is an inactive precursor that must be converted by ACE before exerting effects.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Bradykinin is an inflammatory mediator causing vasodilation and bronchoconstriction, unrelated to thirst.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Renin is the protease that cleaves angiotensinogen; it has no direct hypothalamic action.

questions.stem: A 71-year-old woman with heart failure is started on enalapril. By lowering angiotensin II, the drug reduces aldosterone secretion. In addition to reducing potassium secretion by principal cells, decreased aldosterone reduces hydrogen ion secretion by which of the following renal cell types?

explanation.summary: Aldosterone stimulates H+ secretion by alpha intercalated cells via H+ ATPase activity.
explanation.whyCorrect: In the RAAS pathway, aldosterone acts on the alpha intercalated cell to increase H+ secretion (via increased H+ ATPase activity) and on the principal cell to increase sodium reabsorption and potassium secretion. Lowering aldosterone with an ACE inhibitor therefore reduces both potassium and hydrogen ion secretion.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Afferent arteriolar smooth muscle regulates renal blood flow and is not an aldosterone target for acid secretion.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Juxtaglomerular cells release renin; they do not secrete hydrogen ions.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Macula densa cells sense sodium chloride delivery and signal renin release; they are not aldosterone-responsive acid-secreting cells.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Angiotensin II, not aldosterone, acts on the proximal convoluted tubule to increase Na+/H+ activity and reabsorb sodium, bicarbonate, and water.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man with hypertension is switched from an ACE inhibitor to an ARB at the same guideline-recommended dose because of a dry cough. At follow-up his blood pressure reduction is somewhat smaller than it was on the ACE inhibitor. Which of the following best explains why ACE inhibitors tend to be more potent antihypertensives than ARBs?

choices.label: A
choices.text: ACE inhibitors also block angiotensin II type 1 receptors directly

choices.label: B
choices.text: ACE inhibitors reduce aldosterone but ARBs do not affect aldosterone

choices.label: C
choices.text: ARBs are degraded by ACE in the lungs before reaching their target

choices.label: D
choices.text: ARBs increase renin release, which overrides receptor blockade

choices.label: E
choices.text: ARBs leave circulating angiotensin II free to act on alternate receptors

explanation.summary: ACE inhibitors decrease angiotensin II production, whereas with ARBs circulating angiotensin II can still act on alternate angiotensin receptors.
explanation.whyCorrect: Blocking the conversion of angiotensin I to II leads to an overall decrease in angiotensin II production, which is not the case with ARBs. The circulating angiotensin II that remains during ARB therapy can still produce some vasoconstrictive effects on alternate angiotensin receptors. Clinically, ACE inhibitors therefore tend to be more potent (greater blood pressure reduction) but may carry more side effects.

whyWrongByChoice.A: ACE inhibitors act on the enzyme, not the receptor; receptor blockade is the ARB mechanism.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Both classes reduce aldosterone secretion and decrease potassium secretion; this is a shared effect, not a difference.
whyWrongByChoice.C: ARBs are not degraded by ACE; the difference lies in whether angiotensin II production is decreased.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The brick attributes the potency difference to residual angiotensin II acting on alternate receptors, not to a renin surge.

questions.stem: A pharmacist is reviewing a list of antihypertensive prescriptions. Based on drug nomenclature, which of the following agents blocks the angiotensin II receptor rather than inhibiting angiotensin-converting enzyme?

explanation.summary: ARBs end in -sartan; ACE inhibitors end in -pril.
explanation.whyCorrect: ACE inhibitors and ARBs have an easily recognizable nomenclature: ACE inhibitors end with the suffix -pril, and ARBs end with the suffix -sartan. Candesartan, along with valsartan and losartan, is an ARB.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Benazepril ends in -pril and is an ACE inhibitor.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Captopril ends in -pril and is an ACE inhibitor.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Enalapril ends in -pril and is an ACE inhibitor.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Ramipril ends in -pril and is an ACE inhibitor.

questions.stem: A 63-year-old woman with hypertension is prescribed aliskiren, the only agent in its class available in the United States. Which of the following steps of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system does this drug directly inhibit?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Binding of aldosterone to principal cells

choices.label: B
choices.text: Binding of angiotensin II to its type 1 receptor

choices.label: C
choices.text: Cleavage of angiotensinogen to angiotensin I

choices.label: D
choices.text: Conversion of angiotensin I to angiotensin II

choices.label: E
choices.text: Degradation of bradykinin in the lungs

explanation.summary: Aliskiren is a renin inhibitor that blocks cleavage of angiotensinogen into angiotensin I.
explanation.whyCorrect: Renin inhibitors block the activity of renin, the protease that cleaves angiotensinogen into angiotensin I at the very start of the pathway. Aliskiren is the only renin inhibitor available in the US, and because of its low use in clinical practice the brick focuses on ACE inhibitors and ARBs.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Aliskiren acts at renin, upstream of aldosterone; it does not block aldosterone at its target cells.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Blocking the angiotensin II type 1 receptor is the ARB mechanism.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Blocking conversion of angiotensin I to II is the ACE inhibitor mechanism.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Bradykinin degradation is blocked by ACE inhibitors, not renin inhibitors.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man is discharged two weeks after an acute myocardial infarction. His regimen includes aspirin, a statin, and a beta-blocker. Which of the following additional medication classes is considered first-line therapy in this setting to prevent ventricular fibrosis and abnormal cardiac remodeling?

explanation.summary: ACE inhibitors or ARBs are first-line after myocardial infarction, along with aspirin, statins, and beta-blockers.
explanation.whyCorrect: For patients following a myocardial infarction, ACE inhibitors or ARBs are first-line therapy alongside aspirin, statins, and beta-blockers. Just as in heart failure, they lower angiotensin II and serum aldosterone levels, which can prevent ventricular fibrosis and abnormal cardiac remodeling.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Calcium channel blockers are preferred for hypertension alone in certain patients but are not the post-MI first-line class described.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Loop diuretics are part of the heart failure regimen for fluid management; they are not listed as post-MI first-line therapy to prevent remodeling.
whyWrongByChoice.D: NSAIDs are to be avoided with RAAS inhibitors because of the risk of acute kidney injury.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Renin inhibitors have low clinical use and are not part of the post-MI regimen described.

questions.stem: A 64-year-old man with long-standing type 2 diabetes and diabetic kidney disease is started on losartan. Two weeks later his serum potassium is 6.0 mEq/L. Which of the following features of his underlying kidney disease most increases his susceptibility to this adverse effect?

explanation.summary: Patients with diabetic kidney disease have low renin secretion, placing them at higher risk of hyperkalemia with RAAS inhibitors.
explanation.whyCorrect: RAAS inhibition reduces aldosterone secretion, which reduces renal tubular potassium secretion and can cause hyperkalemia. This is especially likely in patients already at risk, such as those with CKD, patients with diabetic kidney disease (who have low renin secretion), and those on other potassium-retaining drugs.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Increased aldosterone would promote potassium secretion and protect against hyperkalemia, the opposite of the risk described.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Bradykinin metabolism relates to cough and angioedema, not to potassium handling.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Efferent tone relates to GFR maintenance, not to the baseline potassium risk in diabetic kidney disease.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Increased potassium excretion would lower serum potassium; the problem in these patients is reduced excretion.

questions.stem: A 69-year-old man with heart failure and chronic kidney disease is started on enalapril. Three days later his serum creatinine has risen modestly from baseline, and he is otherwise well, euvolemic, and not taking NSAIDs or potassium-sparing agents. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Add an ARB to compensate for the reduced renal effect

choices.label: B
choices.text: Continue the drug and recheck renal function over the next week

choices.label: C
choices.text: Discontinue the drug permanently and document intolerance

choices.label: D
choices.text: Double the enalapril dose to overcome the creatinine rise

choices.label: E
choices.text: Replace enalapril with a renin inhibitor immediately

explanation.summary: An early fall in GFR after starting an ACE inhibitor usually returns to normal within 7-10 days; dose reduction or discontinuation is reserved for cases where it does not.
explanation.whyCorrect: The fall in GFR from efferent arteriolar dilation often occurs within the first few days of starting an ACE inhibitor or ARB, and in most patients GFR returns to normal in 7-10 days. Only if it does not should the dose be reduced or discontinued. Given the importance of these drugs in CKD and heart failure, an initial decrease in GFR may be acceptable in light of their positive long-term effects.

whyWrongByChoice.A: ACE inhibitors and ARBs should not be combined; doing so adds hyperkalemia and AKI risk without additional benefit.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Permanent discontinuation is not indicated for an expected, early, modest GFR decline; the brick reserves dose reduction or discontinuation for GFR that fails to recover.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Increasing the dose would further dilate the efferent arteriole and worsen the GFR decline.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Renin inhibitors also dilate the efferent arteriole and reduce GFR; switching does not address the expected early decline.

questions.stem: A 59-year-old woman has taken ramipril for hypertension for three years without complaint. Over the past two months she has developed a persistent dry, hacking cough that is bothersome and affecting her quality of life. Evaluation reveals no infection or lung disease. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Add a beta-blocker to the current regimen

choices.label: B
choices.text: Add an ARB to ramipril to reduce the cough

choices.label: C
choices.text: Continue ramipril and add an NSAID for symptom relief

choices.label: D
choices.text: Stop all antihypertensive therapy for one month

choices.label: E
choices.text: Switch to a different ACE inhibitor or an ARB

explanation.summary: ACE inhibitor cough can appear even years into therapy and is managed by switching to a different ACE inhibitor or an ARB.
explanation.whyCorrect: The dry cough from bradykinin accumulation can show up at any time, even years after a patient has been taking the medication. There are differences in cough incidence among the various ACE inhibitors, and ARBs have a reduced incidence because they do not affect bradykinin breakdown. If a patient experiences a bothersome dry cough, switching to a different ACE inhibitor or an ARB can alleviate it.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Adding a beta-blocker does nothing to address bradykinin accumulation and leaves the cough untreated.
whyWrongByChoice.B: ACE inhibitors and ARBs should not be combined; the ACE inhibitor causing the cough would remain on board.
whyWrongByChoice.C: NSAIDs should be avoided with ACE inhibitors because the combination increases the risk of acute kidney injury.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Stopping all antihypertensive therapy is unnecessary; switching within the RAAS-inhibiting classes resolves the cough while maintaining control.

questions.stem: A 48-year-old man taking lisinopril presents with swelling of the lips and tongue without urticaria or pruritus. In ACE inhibitor-associated angioedema, accumulated bradykinin binds receptors in the vascular endothelium and stimulates release of which of the following neuropeptides that helps mediate the inflammatory response?

explanation.summary: Bradykinin-driven angioedema involves endothelial receptor binding and release of substance P.
explanation.whyCorrect: ACE inhibitors block the degradation of bradykinin. The large buildup of bradykinin can bind to receptors in the vascular endothelium, which stimulates release of substance P, a neuropeptide that helps mediate the inflammatory response in the body, and induces angioedema affecting the upper airways, face, lips, and tongue.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Aldosterone is a mineralocorticoid governing sodium and potassium handling, not an inflammatory neuropeptide.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Angiotensin II levels fall with ACE inhibition and it is not released by endothelial bradykinin receptor activation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Histamine is not the mediator the brick describes for ACE inhibitor angioedema; the pathway is bradykinin and substance P.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Prostaglandins such as PGE2 dilate the afferent arteriole and are relevant to the NSAID interaction, not to angioedema.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old African American man is diagnosed with stage 1 hypertension. He has no history of heart failure, myocardial infarction, diabetes, or kidney disease. Which of the following is generally the most preferred first-line agent for this patient?

explanation.summary: For hypertension alone in an African American patient, a dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker such as amlodipine is generally the preferred first-line agent.
explanation.whyCorrect: African American patients have a 4.5 times greater risk of ACE inhibitor-induced angioedema than Caucasians. If treating hypertension alone in an African American patient, a dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker (e.g., amlodipine) will generally be the most preferred first-line agent.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Aliskiren has low clinical use and is not the preferred first-line agent described.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Captopril is an ACE inhibitor and carries the same elevated angioedema risk as lisinopril.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Lisinopril is an ACE inhibitor, the class with the markedly elevated angioedema risk in this population.
whyWrongByChoice.E: An ARB trial is reserved for African American patients whose hypertension is accompanied by comorbid conditions such as heart failure.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old African American woman has hypertension and heart failure with reduced ejection fraction. Her physician is weighing the benefit of RAAS inhibition against her elevated risk of drug-induced angioedema. Which of the following is the most appropriate approach?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Avoid all RAAS inhibitors regardless of comorbidity

choices.label: B
choices.text: Combine an ACE inhibitor with an ARB at low doses

choices.label: C
choices.text: Substitute a renin inhibitor for both classes

choices.label: D
choices.text: Trial an ARB with close monitoring

choices.label: E
choices.text: Use a dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker alone

explanation.summary: When an African American patient has hypertension with comorbid heart failure, a trial of an ARB with close monitoring is generally warranted.
explanation.whyCorrect: Although a dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker is preferred for hypertension alone in African American patients because of the 4.5-fold higher angioedema risk with ACE inhibitors, comorbid conditions like heart failure change the calculus. In that setting a trial with an ARB, which has a lower risk of angioedema and cough, together with close monitoring, is generally warranted.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Avoiding RAAS inhibition entirely forgoes first-line heart failure therapy; the brick recommends an ARB trial with monitoring instead.
whyWrongByChoice.B: ACE inhibitors and ARBs should not be combined because of additive hyperkalemia, AKI, and angioedema risk without added benefit.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Renin inhibitors have low clinical use and are not the recommended approach for heart failure described in the brick.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A calcium channel blocker alone is preferred only when hypertension is the sole problem; it does not provide the heart failure benefits of RAAS inhibition.

questions.stem: A 74-year-old man on lisinopril for hypertension is prescribed triamterene by another provider. Two weeks later his serum potassium is 6.2 mEq/L. Which of the following best describes how triamterene compounded the potassium-retaining effect of his ACE inhibitor?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It antagonizes aldosterone at its receptor

choices.label: B
choices.text: It blocks sodium channels in the renal tubule

choices.label: E
choices.text: It suppresses renin release from the kidney

explanation.summary: Amiloride and triamterene are sodium channel blockers that worsen ACE inhibitor-induced hyperkalemia.
explanation.whyCorrect: On their own, ACE inhibitors and ARBs can cause hyperkalemia, but this is worsened when they are taken with other potassium-retaining agents. The brick lists aldosterone antagonists (spironolactone), sodium channel blockers (amiloride and triamterene), and potassium supplements. Triamterene belongs to the sodium channel blocker group.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Aldosterone receptor antagonism is the mechanism of spironolactone, a different potassium-retaining agent.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Blocking bradykinin degradation is the ACE inhibitor effect responsible for cough and angioedema.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Inhibiting prostaglandin synthesis is the NSAID mechanism that raises the risk of acute kidney injury, not triamterene's action.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Suppressing renin release is the action of a renin inhibitor, not triamterene.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old woman taking candesartan for hypertension asks whether she can begin an over-the-counter oral potassium supplement that a friend recommended for leg cramps. Adding the supplement to her current therapy would most increase her risk of which of the following?

explanation.summary: Potassium supplements taken with an ACE inhibitor or ARB increase the risk of hyperkalemia.
explanation.whyCorrect: ARBs reduce aldosterone secretion and therefore reduce renal potassium secretion. Oral potassium supplements are one of the agents the brick lists that worsen this effect, alongside aldosterone antagonists and sodium channel blocker diuretics. ACE inhibitors and ARBs should not be used alongside oral potassium supplements because of the hyperkalemia risk.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Angioedema is related to bradykinin accumulation, which potassium supplements do not affect.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Bronchial smooth muscle contraction is a bradykinin effect, not a consequence of potassium supplementation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Dry cough is a bradykinin effect of ACE inhibitors and is not influenced by potassium intake.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Teratogenicity relates to RAAS inhibitor use in pregnancy, not to potassium supplementation.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man with hypertension is well controlled on lisinopril but requires an additional medication for a new comorbid condition. Which of the following classes is commonly used together with an ACE inhibitor without producing a notable drug interaction?

explanation.summary: Beta-blockers, calcium channel blockers, and loop diuretics are commonly combined with ACE inhibitors or ARBs without notable interactions.
explanation.whyCorrect: Beta-blockers, calcium channel blockers, and loop diuretics are all commonly used in combination with ACE inhibitors and ARBs and do not produce notable drug interactions. Beta-blockers in particular are part of the first-line regimens for heart failure and post-myocardial infarction alongside RAAS inhibitors.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Aldosterone antagonists such as spironolactone worsen ACE inhibitor-induced hyperkalemia.
whyWrongByChoice.C: NSAIDs constrict the afferent arteriole and, combined with efferent dilation from an ACE inhibitor, greatly increase the risk of acute kidney injury.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Oral potassium supplements are listed as agents that worsen hyperkalemia with ACE inhibitors and ARBs.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Sodium channel blockers such as amiloride and triamterene worsen hyperkalemia when combined with RAAS inhibitors.

questions.stem: A 67-year-old man cannot tolerate an ACE inhibitor and is switched to valsartan. His physician counsels him that the ARB will avoid some but not all of the adverse effects of his previous drug. Which of the following adverse effects occurs at a similar rate with ARBs as with ACE inhibitors?

explanation.summary: ARBs share the hyperkalemia and acute kidney injury risks of ACE inhibitors but have a lower risk of cough and angioedema.
explanation.whyCorrect: ARBs have similar net effects to ACE inhibitors on the efferent arteriole and on decreased potassium secretion, so hyperkalemia and acute kidney injury occur with both classes. Because ACE inhibition is not involved, ARBs do not cause bradykinin accumulation and therefore have a lower risk of dry cough and angioedema.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Angioedema is a bradykinin-mediated effect that is less common with ARBs than with ACE inhibitors.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Bronchial smooth muscle contraction is a bradykinin effect underlying the ACE inhibitor cough and is not shared by ARBs.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Dry cough is a bradykinin effect; ARBs have a reduced incidence because they do not block bradykinin degradation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Increased vascular permeability is a bradykinin effect and is not a feature of ARB therapy.

questions.stem: In the final step of the renin-angiotensin system, angiotensin II stimulates the adrenal gland to release a hormone whose important role is expanding blood volume. Which of the following is that hormone?

explanation.summary: Angiotensin II stimulates aldosterone release from the adrenal gland, and aldosterone expands blood volume.
explanation.whyCorrect: The fourth step of the RAAS pathway is release of aldosterone: angiotensin II stimulates release of aldosterone from the adrenal gland, and aldosterone has an important role in expanding blood volume by promoting renal sodium reabsorption. The RAAS primarily determines serum levels of aldosterone and angiotensin II.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Angiotensin I is the precursor formed when renin cleaves angiotensinogen, before ACE converts it to angiotensin II.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Angiotensinogen is the inactive precursor protein made by the liver at the start of the pathway.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Bradykinin is an inflammatory mediator degraded by ACE; it is not an adrenal hormone.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Substance P is a neuropeptide involved in angioedema, not an adrenal volume-expanding hormone.

questions.stem: A 57-year-old man with hypertension is started on benazepril. Beyond its vascular and adrenal effects, angiotensin II normally acts directly on the proximal convoluted tubule to promote reabsorption of sodium, bicarbonate, and water. Reduced angiotensin II from benazepril decreases the activity of which of the following in the proximal tubule?

choices.label: C
choices.text: H+ ATPase in alpha intercalated cells

explanation.summary: Angiotensin II increases Na+/H+ activity in the proximal convoluted tubule, driving sodium, bicarbonate, and water reabsorption.
explanation.whyCorrect: In the RAAS pathway diagram, angiotensin II acts on the proximal convoluted tubule cell to increase Na+/H+ activity, which permits reabsorption of sodium, bicarbonate, and water (and permits contraction alkalosis). Lowering angiotensin II with an ACE inhibitor reduces this proximal reabsorption.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Aquaporin-mediated water reabsorption in the collecting duct is driven by ADH from the posterior pituitary.
whyWrongByChoice.B: ENaC activity in principal cells is increased by aldosterone, not by angiotensin II acting on the proximal tubule.
whyWrongByChoice.C: H+ ATPase in alpha intercalated cells is stimulated by aldosterone in the collecting duct, not by angiotensin II in the proximal tubule.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Na+/K+ ATPase in principal cells is an aldosterone-driven collecting duct effect.

questions.stem: Renin secretion by the juxtaglomerular cells is regulated by several signals arising from the kidney and the nervous system. Which of the following stimuli promotes renin release?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Increased pressure at the renal baroreceptors

choices.label: D
choices.text: Increased sodium chloride delivery to the macula densa

choices.label: E
choices.text: Increased sympathetic tone at beta-1 receptors

explanation.summary: Renin release is triggered by decreased renal perfusion pressure, decreased NaCl delivery to the macula densa, and increased sympathetic tone via beta-1 receptors.
explanation.whyCorrect: The RAAS pathway lists three triggers for renin release from the juxtaglomerular cells: decreased blood pressure sensed by renal baroreceptors, decreased Na+/Cl- delivery to the macula densa cells, and increased sympathetic tone acting through beta-1 receptors. Of the options, only increased sympathetic tone stimulates renin.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Low blood volume triggers renin release; increased blood volume does not.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Decreased pressure at the renal baroreceptors stimulates renin; increased pressure suppresses it.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Increased renal blood flow is the opposite of the low-flow state that juxtaglomerular cells sense to release renin.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Decreased, not increased, sodium chloride delivery to the macula densa promotes renin release.

questions.stem: A 76-year-old woman with heart failure develops a rise in serum creatinine within days of starting valsartan. Urinalysis is bland and renal ultrasonography shows no hydronephrosis. The acute kidney injury caused by ARBs in this setting is best classified as which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Intrinsic, from deposition of drug crystals within the tubules

choices.label: B
choices.text: Intrinsic, from direct toxic injury to tubular epithelial cells

choices.label: C
choices.text: Intrinsic, from immune-mediated inflammation of the glomerulus

choices.label: D
choices.text: Postrenal, from obstruction of urine outflow beyond the kidney

choices.label: E
choices.text: Prerenal, from reduced filtration pressure arising before the kidney

explanation.summary: ACE inhibitor and ARB-induced AKI is prerenal, caused by a hemodynamic fall in GFR rather than structural kidney damage.
explanation.whyCorrect: Dilation of the efferent arteriole by RAAS inhibitors acutely decreases GFR, especially in low-flow states like dehydration or heart failure. This is a form of prerenal acute kidney injury: prerenal refers to a cause occurring before the kidney, most often reduced blood flow to the kidneys that lowers their ability to filter blood appropriately.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Crystal deposition is not a mechanism of RAAS inhibitor kidney injury.
whyWrongByChoice.B: RAAS inhibitors do not directly poison tubular cells; the injury is a change in filtration pressure.
whyWrongByChoice.C: There is no immune-mediated glomerular inflammation; the bland urinalysis and mechanism point to a hemodynamic cause.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Postrenal injury involves obstruction of urine outflow; the normal ultrasound and the hemodynamic mechanism exclude this.

questions.stem: A 61-year-old man with chronic kidney disease and proteinuria has a mild dry cough on lisinopril. He understands the drug slows progression of his kidney disease and asks whether it is safe to keep taking it despite the cough. Which of the following is the most accurate counseling?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The cough indicates a bronchial infection that requires antibiotic treatment

choices.label: B
choices.text: The cough is a warning sign of impending angioedema, so the drug must be stopped

choices.label: C
choices.text: The cough itself has no deleterious consequences, so continuing is reasonable if tolerable

choices.label: D
choices.text: The cough means he should add an ARB to protect his kidneys further

choices.label: E
choices.text: The cough will resolve within days if the lisinopril dose is doubled

explanation.summary: ACE inhibitor cough is troublesome but harmless, so patients may choose to tolerate it for the drug's long-term benefits.
explanation.whyCorrect: The dry cough is caused by bradykinin accumulation and can be a troublesome side effect for many patients. However, given the positive long-term benefits of ACE inhibitors, some patients will choose to tolerate this side effect because there are no deleterious consequences of the cough itself. If it becomes intolerable, switching to a different ACE inhibitor or an ARB is an option.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The cough is a drug side effect from bradykinin, not an infection; antibiotics are not indicated.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Although both are bradykinin-mediated, the brick does not describe cough as a precursor to angioedema, and the cough has no deleterious consequences.
whyWrongByChoice.D: ACE inhibitors and ARBs should not be combined; adding an ARB increases hyperkalemia and AKI risk without additional benefit.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Increasing the dose would not relieve a bradykinin-mediated cough and offers no described benefit.
